(c) H types 1 and 2 are the terminal moieties expressed in histo-blood group type O individuals, but in types A, B and AB individuals the H antigens are further modified by enzymes that transfer N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc, type A), Gal (type B), or either carbohydrate (type AB) to the terminal Gal residue of an H antigen in α1,3 linkage. ABH, Lewis and secretor phenotypes and enzymatic pathways are described in greater detail in other reviews 55, 56.Figure 3The small intestinal gut section shows the villi projecting into the lumen (top) with the crypts beneath the villi. Within the crypts are the progenitor stem cells of the small intestine. Crypt stem cell division supplies cells that differentiate as they are pushed down into the base of the crypt, becoming paneth cells, or up into the villus, becoming goblet cells or enterocytes. Paneth cells at the base of the crypt secrete lysozyme, goblet cells secrete mucins, undifferentiated enterocytes secrete chloride ions, and differentiated enterocytes absorb nutrients from the gut lumen until they undergo apoptosis and are sloughed off the villus. As enterocytes differentiate and travel up the villus, they express higher amounts and a greater variety of carbohydrates, including ABH and Lewis histo-blood group antigens [55]. Further description of these and other specialized intestinal cells can be found elsewhere [73].NV VLPs show the strongest level of binding when interacting with the H type 1 [also know as Lewis(d) or Led] synthetic carbohydrate antigen (Table 1; Figure 2a) 50, 52. H type 1 oligosaccharides are also best at inhibiting NV VLP binding to enterocytes, red blood cells (RBCs) and synthetic carbohydrate 50, 53. The Leb antigen differs from H type 1 only by the presence of a fucose in α1–4 linkage to the most distal N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) of a carbohydrate chain (Figure 2). The binding of NV VLPs appears to be minimally affected by this additional fucose, because Leb closely follows H type 1 in strength of binding to synthetic carbohydrates and hemagglutination inhibition 50, 52. Both H type 1 and Leb carbohydrates are found in saliva and other mucosal secretions from individuals who are Lewis-positive secretors (Figure 2). NV VLPs bind to saliva from all secretor-positive individuals, and their saliva can inhibit VLPs from binding to enterocytes and saliva 52, 53, 54. Hemagglutination and synthetic carbohydrate-binding show that H type 2 and 3 carbohydrates also bind to NV VLPs and can inhibit homologous and heterologous carbohydrate-binding 50, 52, 53. Furthermore, the heterologous inhibition between H and Lewis antigens suggests that these carbohydrates bind NV VLPs at the same site [50]. NV VLPs also bind type A and AB RBCs, and type A saliva and synthetic carbohydrate, but they do not bind B antigen synthetic carbohydrate nor do they bind the majority of type B RBCs and saliva 49, 50, 52, 54. The A carbohydrate antigen is dissimilar to the H and Lewis antigens. To date, it is unclear if the NV VLPs bind the H antigen segment of the A antigen (Figure 2) or if the A antigen interacts at a distinct site on the NV VLP. The A, but not B, trisaccharide antigens bind the VLPs, however the H disaccharide does not bind VLPs well compared with that of the H and A trisaccharides [54]. This suggests that there might be a unique A antigen-binding site on the NV VLPs.To date, the carbohydrate-binding of one GI and seven GII norovirus VLPs have been reported, with the single GI NV VLPs binding to carbohydrates being the most thoroughly studied interaction (Table 1). The GII VLPs bind to the same group of carbohydrate antigens as NV VLPs, but their binding specificities are different. In addition, the carbohydrate-binding properties of GII VLPs are varied. For example, VLPs from VA387 norovirus (GII.4, clustered with the current predominant circulating norovirus strains) binds saliva and synthetic carbohydrates of all secretors regardless of their ABO type, whereas the VLPs from Snow Mountain virus (GII.2) bind the saliva of secretors of types B and AB, but not of types O and A 52, 54. It remains to be determined if the carbohydrate-binding profiles correlate with genetic clusters within a norovirus genogroup, or if the carbohydrate-binding properties are more strain-specific. Finding the carbohydrate-binding sites on noroviruses and identifying residues that are important for binding should help predict the carbohydrate-binding characteristics of a norovirus on the basis of its amino acid sequence. However, if noroviruses are consistent with many carbohydrate-binding proteins, the three-dimensional nature of the binding pocket could complicate binding predictions based on linear sequence and antigenic properties 57, 58.From previous volunteer challenge studies, there is strong evidence that carbohydrate-binding is essential for NV infection. Individuals who are non-secretors (Se−), who do not express the FUT2 fucosyltransferase and consequently do not make H type 1 or Leb (Figure 2a), do not become infected after challenge with NV [49]. Furthermore, individuals expressing the B antigen are less likely to be infected by NV; however, when type B individuals are infected they are asymptomatic [59]. This strongly supports the hypothesis that carbohydrate-binding is crucial for NV replication, because NV VLPs show strongest binding to H type 1 and Leb carbohydrates, and minimal binding to type B RBCs and saliva 50, 52. Even though the number of people in each secretor and ABO phenotype is low, especially for type B, these associations have been subsequently confirmed by other volunteer challenge studies (A.M. Hutson et al., unpublished).Therefore, we predict that secretors of types O and A are at greatest risk of NV infection and disease. Because other noroviruses display different ABH and Lewis carbohydrate-binding profiles 52, 54, individuals resistant to NV infection could be susceptible to other norovirus strains. If carbohydrate-binding is conserved within genetic clusters, this could help explain the wide prevalence of GII.4 noroviruses, where the broad range of carbohydrates to which the VA387 virus binds increases the proportion of susceptible individuals within the population. These data also help to explain why the absence of antibodies to a norovirus strain does not necessarily predict susceptibility to infection with that virus strain. Persons without NV-specific antibodies could be completely resistant to infection because of the lack of expression of carbohydrates necessary for virus attachment to host cells. Conversely, the presence of norovirus-specific antibodies could indicate previous infection and therefore susceptibility at the virus–receptor binding level. As with many mucosal infections, a single norovirus infection does not appear to provide long-term protection [60]. Without re-exposure to a particular norovirus strain, protection wanes after six months and it has been reported that susceptible individuals have been reinfected two years after prior exposure [48]. However, multiple exposures to the virus can result in induction of protective immunity and establishes a rationale for vaccine development 60, 61. A recent study has suggested that production of NV-specific salivary IgA early in infection might be associated with protection against more severe disease [49]. These data support the development of a norovirus vaccine that generates a strong mucosal immune response.Further evidence supporting the biological relevance of NV VLP–carbohydrate interaction comes from the presence of antibodies in convalescent sera that specifically block the binding of VLP to carbohydrate. For influenza A virus, the capacity of antibodies to specifically block the virus binding to its cellular receptor (sialic acid) shows better correlation with levels of protection from influenza A challenge than the total amount of antibodies that can recognize the virus but that might not interfere with receptor-binding [62]. Therefore, if binding of NV to H antigen is essential for virus infection, then antibodies that inhibit NV receptor interactions will probably develop in response to infection. Notably, hemagglutination inhibition and antiserum blockade assays demonstrated that the convalescent phase sera of NV-infected individuals have more NV–H antigen blocking antibodies than pre-challenge serum samples 50, 52. The presence of antibodies that inhibit this binding could be associated with protection from NV infection or disease.ABH and Lewis carbohydrates are used by other mucosal pathogens. For example, the bacteria Helicobacter pylori and Staphylococcus aureus attach to cells through H and Lewis carbohydrates (Table 2). However, the ABH and Lewis carbohydrate-binding specificity has only been described for viruses in the Caliciviridae family. Rabbit hemorrhagic disease virus (RHDV) was the first calicivirus shown to bind H type 2 carbohydrate [63]. RHDV is distantly related to noroviruses and causes a respiratory infection in rabbits that spreads systemically with high replication in the liver, causing internal hemorrhaging and death. The H type 2 carbohydrate is expressed on rabbit lung epithelia, but its role in RHDV infection remains to be determined. Binding of H and Lewis carbohydrates could be a common theme in calicivirus–cell interactions, but such binding interactions have not been shown for viruses in the Vesivirus or Sapovirus genera. RHDV, feline calicivirus (vesivirus) and porcine enteric calicivirus (sapovirus) are systemic pathogens 64, 65, 66. For human noroviruses, replication and pathogenesis have only been described in the gut and norovirus has not been identified in the sera of infected individuals. However, because NV VLPs bind H type 2 and Lewis antigens, which are found on erythrocytes and other circulating and vascular cells, the possibility of systemic spread of NV should be reexamined with more sensitive molecular tests.In the human gut, the developmental and differentiation-dependent nature of H and Lewis antigen expression on enterocytes, combined with the uniqueness of this virus–carbohydrate interaction, suggests that noroviruses are very selective in their binding to cells and that virus replication might be cell-type dependent. This could help explain the difficulty in adapting noroviruses to growth in cell culture. Potential host cells could be transfected with glycotransferases to enable the expression of norovirus-binding carbohydrates. This has been achieved with Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells, which normally do not express H antigen carbohydrates and show little binding of NV VLPs [53]. When the CHO cells were transfected with the rat FTB gene, the rat homolog to human FUT2, they expressed H type 1 and were able to bind NV VLPs [53]. However, the lack of carbohydrate expression does not explain the block to NV replication. Caco-2 cells, a human cell line that expresses markers of differentiated enterocytes that are characteristic of small intestinal cells, do express H types 1 and 2 [67]. These cells bind to rNV VLPs more efficiently than other cell lines that have been tested, but they do not support NV replication [51]. This suggests that a co-receptor could be required for sufficient norovirus entry, or that the block in viral replication in Caco-2 cells occurs at a post-binding step.In secretor-positive individuals, ABH and Lewis antigens are found on epithelial cell surfaces and secreted mucins (heavily glycosylated glycoproteins) in saliva, milk and other mucous secretions. Because NV VLPs can bind free oligosaccharides, the role of these secreted antigens, which could bind NV and potentially inhibit infection, is uncertain. Even with secreted carbohydrates potentially binding NV VLPs, secretor-positive individuals are reported to be more susceptible to NV infection [49]. One explanation for this apparent contradiction is related to the multivalent nature of carbohydrate expression on cells that interact with multiple binding sites on VLPs. As with other carbohydrate-binding proteins, the affinity of NV VLPs for free monomeric oligosaccharides appears to be low [53]. This suggests that the avidity of binding of VLP to H and Lewis carbohydrates on a cell surface is a more biologically relevant event. Furthermore, for a multivalent viral or bacterial protein the monomeric affinity between its carbohydrate ligand and the monomeric protein is generally low [68]. Too high an affinity between a virus and its cellular receptor can inhibit the dissemination and consequently the viability of the virus [69]. Therefore, the strength or weakness of the binding of a norovirus strain to cellular carbohydrates could affect susceptibility within a population, virulence within an infected person and transmissibility to others.4Questions for future norovirus researchThis new information on norovirus epidemiology and host susceptibility factors leads to many new questions about infection with these viruses. What is the nature of the norovirus carbohydrate-binding site? To date, it is known that the carbohydrate-binding epitope on NV can be found in the P domain and is conformation-dependent [50]. Additionally, all carbohydrate-binding studies have been done using VLPs. Therefore, even though the NV volunteer challenge studies indicate that similarities exist between the binding of VLP and native virus, it is unknown whether norovirus virions have the same carbohydrate-binding properties as their VLP counterparts. Knowledge of the receptor-binding site for these viruses could lead to the development of antiviral carbohydrate analogs for prophylactic use in especially sensitive situations, such as in military, hospital or nursing home settings, or for treatment of individuals who are frail or immunocompromised.What blocks norovirus replication in cultured cells? Finding potential receptor(s) for NV could aid in identifying cells or tissues that are susceptible to NV infection and could help explain one level of host tropism for this non-cultivatable virus. Because H antigens are expressed on Caco-2 cells, a lack of carbohydrate receptors is not the block in NV replication in these cells. There could be a co-receptor missing on Caco-2 and other cells, the presence of which increases NV internalization. Alternatively, other factors downstream of viral entry might be missing, or factors that interfere in NV replication could be expressed in cultured cells. Recently, a murine calicivirus was identified that is closely related to noroviruses by sequence analysis [18]. This virus infects mice orally, causing a systemic infection without gastroenteritis. Studies with this small animal model of infection are expected to provide new information about essential host and viral factors that are important for pathogenesis by making use of knockout and transgenic mice, and possibly recombinant viruses. Initial studies have indicated that immunocompromised mice become persistently infected and that the innate immune response plays an important role in the outcome of murine norovirus infection. The role of the innate immune response in human norovirus replication and pathogenesis also needs to be examined.Do cross-species norovirus infections occur naturally? GI and GII noroviruses were initially only isolated from humans. Recently, phylogenetic analysis has indicated that other caliciviruses that infect cattle, pigs and mice also fall within the Norovirus genus 14, 15, 16, 17, 18. These viruses form their own genogroups or genetic clusters within GI and GII, but the number of animal noroviruses that have been characterized remains relatively small compared with the number of human norovirus strains. The classification of animal caliciviruses within the Norovirus genus raises the question of whether zoonotic infections occur. Answering this question is important, because cross-species infections would affect the epidemiology and evolution of these viruses and complicate our ability to block transmission by vaccination or other therapy [14].How can norovirus outbreaks and sporadic infections be prevented? Currently, good personal hygiene is the best preventative action against norovirus infection. Washing hands frequently and thoroughly and disinfecting contaminated surfaces with a 5–10% solution of household bleach in water, especially after contact with persons showing norovirus symptoms, is the best defense. People who are ill should refrain from preparing food for others, and once symptoms clear, they should be aware that they could still shed virus for up to three weeks. Furthermore, steps should be taken to keep water and food supplies free from noroviruses.Currently, candidate vaccines are being tested for use in preventing norovirus disease 70, 71. Also, progress is being made to determine the location and structure of the NV-carbohydrate binding site for developing possible antivirals. These studies will help in the development of therapies to reduce norovirus illness and transmission, especially in nursing home, hospital and military settings.


Title: Recent insights into reverse genetics of norovirus

1Introduction1.1Norovirus biologyNorovirus is predominant etiological agent of non-bacterial gastroenteritis and is associated with approximately one in five cases of all gastroenteritis worldwide. Transmission of norovirus is primarily through the consumption of contaminated food or water as well as by aerosolization. Norovirus is highly contagious and individuals at all ages are vulnerable, especially in immunocompromised populations, where infection may lead to severe clinical outcomes (Mattner et al., 2006; Frange et al., 2012; Green, 2014; Ye et al., 2015; Bok et al., 2016). People infected with norovirus usually have a rapid onset of symptoms, including diarrhea, vomiting, nausea, low-grade fever and abdominal cramps. At a global level, norovirus is responsible for an estimated 685 million diarrheal episodes and 212,000 deaths every year (Lopman et al., 2016; Bányai et al., 2018; Lucero et al., 2021).Norovirus is an RNA virus in the family Caliciviridae, which is characterized by rapid transmission and frequent genome mutation. Norovirus particles are small (27–40 nm in diameter) and nonenveloped that possess a single-stranded, (+) sense genomic RNA of ∼7.5–7.7 kb in length (Fig. 1A). Its genome generally includes three open reading frames (ORFs), except for murine norovirus containing four ORFs (Fig. 1B and C). ORF1 encodes a precursor polyprotein that is then hydrolyzed and cleaved by a protease (NS6) into six non-structural proteins (NS1/2 to NS7). ORF2 encodes the major structural protein (VP1), which is responsible for the viral capsid and can exist in up to 180 copies in the viral particle. VP1 has a shell (S) domain and a protruding (P) domain, with the S domain surrounding the viral RNA and connecting to the P domain by a flexible hinge. The P domain can be subdivided into P1 and P2 subdomains (Prasad et al., 1999). P2 is the key region involved in immunogenicity, which is in the outermost layer of VP1 and enables to recognize histo-blood group antigens (HBGAs) (Tan et al., 2004; Lochridge and Hardy, 2007). As initial attachment factor, HBGAs are closely associated with genetic susceptibility for human norovirus infection, and bile acids functions as a cofactor to enhance HBGA binding for certain norovirus genotypes (Kilic et al., 2019; Tenge et al., 2021). Based on the diversity of amino acid (aa) coding sequences of VP1, norovirus is divided into 10 genogroups (GI-GX) and almost 50 genotypes. GI, GII, GIV, GVIII, and GIX are known to be the main genotypic groups infecting humans (Chhabra et al., 2019). ORF3 encodes the minor structural protein (VP2), which is located inside the virus and is involved in capsid assembly and genome encapsulation (Vongpunsawad et al., 2013).Fig. 1(A) Schematic of the structure of norovirus. The viral capsid consists of VP1, where the shell (S) domain surrounds the viral RNA, and the protruding (P) domain can be divided into P1 and P2 subdomains, and P2 can interact with HBGAs. (B-C) Schematic of the genome structure of norovirus. (B) Human norovirus has three ORFs, which encode six non-structural proteins, VP1 and VP2, respectively. (C) Murine norovirus has one more ORF4 compared to human norovirus, which can encode virulence factor 1 (VF1).Fig. 11.2Transmission and epidemiology of norovirusNorovirus is highly contagious, as even as a few particles can cause illnesses. Transmission of human norovirus occurs by the fecal-oral route, either through the consumption with contaminated food and water or through the exposure to infectious fomites in the environment. As norovirus continues to shed infectious viral particles even after symptoms have resolved, it often leads to nosocomial infections and community outbreaks. Norovirus represents a strong survival capacity and is highly stable in the environment. The persistence of the virus in a closed environment increases the risk of recurrent infections (Lopman et al., 2012). Food-borne transmission is an important route for the rapid dissemination of norovirus. Food chain globalization increases the probability of exchanging recombinants between multiple regions and bring more challenges to recognize foodborne outbreaks of norovirus (de Graaf et al., 2016). In addition to target human host, noroviruses have been detected in the stools of many mammalian species, although their roles as pathogens in those animals remain controversial (van Der Poel et al., 2000; Cheetham et al., 2006; Souza et al., 2008; Li et al., 2021).Norovirus infections occur throughout the year, generally peaking in the fall and winter. Since the first worldwide pandemic of norovirus in 1995–1996, the GII.4 genotype has been endemic and dominant worldwide, causing 50%−70% of norovirus outbreaks each year, and has led to another six pandemics due to its quick mutation (Kroneman et al., 2013; Tohma et al., 2019). However, during the winter of 2014–2015, the previously rare GII.17[P17] norovirus strain emerged and replaced GII.4 Sydney as the dominant genotype threatening many areas in Asian (Chan et al., 2015; Matsushima et al., 2015). In addition, the emergence of the GII.2[P16] variant strain in the 2016 to 2017 epidemic season also led to frequent norovirus outbreaks in various countries (Shen et al., 2020). Meanwhile, since 2015, GII.4 Sydney has been reorganized and GII.4 Sydney[P31] and GII.4 Sydney[P16] have reemerged and spread in multiple countries, with GII.4 Sydney[P31] is prevalent mainly in Asia and GII.4 Sydney[P16] is prominent in Australia and the United States (Lun et al., 2018; Barclay et al., 2019; Chuchaona et al., 2019; Fang et al., 2021b).1.3Genetic diversity of norovirusDue to the extreme diversity presented by norovirus, it can easily evade the host immune response and poses serious threat to human health. GII.4 is the predominant genotype circulating worldwide, with new variants emerging almost every 2–5 years, and the successive accumulation of mutations at antigenic sites on VP1 allows for a shift in antigenic properties, facilitating variants escape from herd immunity (Mallory et al., 2019; Kendra et al., 2021). However, there are times that GII.4 strains retain their phenotypic characteristics for over 5 years, and this is probably attributed to changes in the immune dominance of epitopes associated with neutralizing activity (Parra et al., 2017; Tohma et al., 2022).Besides the highest sequence variability in VP1, emerging dominant strains has been found containing variable motifs that are related to RdRp and other nonstructural proteins. RdRp alteration of fidelity not only affects the pathogenicity of the virus during infection, but also has an impact on virus transmission. High-fidelity polymerases may reduce transmission efficiency, contributing to the genetic diversity (Arias et al., 2016). Furthermore, there is an overlap region about 20 bp between ORF1 and ORF2, and different virulent strains tend to recombine near this overlap region. Thus, norovirus genetic diversity can also be achieved by recombination at the ORF1/ORF2 boundary through genomic exchange between different polymerases and coat proteins.Point mutations and recombination within or between genotypes are the main forms of the genetic evolution of norovirus (White, 2014). While the question of the mechanism driving norovirus evolution remains unresolved, factors such as antigenic drift under herd immune selection pressure, altered polymerase fidelity or lack of herd immunity could be responsible for norovirus evolution (Lindesmith et al., 2008; Lopman et al., 2008). Moreover, new norovirus strains may have a more potent invasive capacity and become pandemic variants owing to their antigenic drift, the emergence of point mutations, and the absence of pre-existing herd immunity (Niendorf et al., 2017).1.4Culture model of norovirusThe absence of robust cellular tissue culture models has hampered the understanding of human norovirus immunity as well as hindered the development of vaccines and antiviral drugs. Murine norovirus model is currently being used in place of human norovirus. Cell culture model of murine norovirus was first developed in 2004 to examine its tropism by culturing in macrophages and dendritic cells (Wobus et al., 2004). Mouse models of murine norovirus are abundant, especially the Stat1−/− and IFNαβγR−/− mouse models that are widely used to examine the host immune response against pathogens (Hsu et al., 2016). Despite numerous challenges in the successful propagation of human norovirus, researchers have continued to spare their efforts on human norovirus in vitro cultivation. In recent year, a cell culture system was established using human norovirus GII.4 Sydney strain to infect human B cells under the stimulating effect of intestinal bacteria and HBGAs (Jones et al., 2014). Besides, human norovirus strains were for the first time cultured in a stem cell-derived, non-transformed human intestinal enteroid (HIE), which laid the foundation for further improvement of human norovirus in vitro culture system (Ettayebi et al., 2016). Landmark achievements in the in vitro culture of human norovirus have been achieved with the application of HIE system to effectively replicate several norovirus genotypes and perform functional analysis (Costantini et al., 2018; Lin et al., 2020; Murakami et al., 2020; Hayashi et al., 2021; Ford-Siltz et al., 2022; Tohma et al., 2022). Due to the complexity of constructing a reproducible HIE model, this system only supports the replication of certain genotypes and is largely influenced by the initial virus titer (Jones et al., 2015; Bhar and Jones, 2019; Ettayebi et al., 2021). Thus, future strides are required to increase the reproducibility and infection levels of the system.1.5A review of norovirus reverse geneticsWhile significant progress has been made in norovirus cultivation, these systems are not sufficiently efficient to propagate human norovirus. The growth of human norovirus in the infection models of B-cell (Jones et al., 2015) and HIE (Ettayebi et al., 2016) were with less than 3.5 and 3.8 log increase, respectively. Development of robust and reliable culture models with desired virus yield is urgently need. The emergence of reverse genetics techniques offers and promise and may consider as a sword to break the dilemma. Reverse genetics approaches focus on genes and create mutants by artificially changing the nucleotide sequences of genes, including mutations, deletions and insertions, to make the genotypes and phenotypes with precise correlation. After decades of development, reverse genetic systems now have been successfully used to rescue various types of viruses, i.e., obtaining infectious virus particles through a series of steps such as cDNA cloning and modification of full-length fragments of the genome, construction of helper plasmids, sequence determination, co-transfection, and identification of virus offspring (Almazán et al., 2014; Schmidt and Mühlberger, 2016; Wang et al., 2021). Therefore, reverse genetic systems to rescue infectious norovirus in vitro allows for studying host pathways, pathogen interactions, and viral protein functions (Asanaka et al., 2005; Arias et al., 2012b; Oliveira et al., 2018; Ludwig-Begall et al., 2020). In this review, we describe recent advances in the study of the reverse genetic system and discuss the application and prospect of this system in norovirus, as a powerful tool for antiviral drug and vaccine development.2Reverse geneticsReverse genetics has developed as a strategy that is complementary but opposing to forward genetics. Forward genetics investigates for genetic mutations that are directly linked to the disease phenotype. This technique is often complex and cumbersome. Conversely, reverse genetics focus on genes to induce the candidate mutants into a model system by artificially altering the nucleotide sequences, including mutations, deletions and insertions, as a way of testing the associations between phenotypes and genotypes of the disease. Based on the high-throughput sequencing technology and revolutionary gene engineering tool, reverse genetics as the recent development of recombinant DNA technology, now provides a powerful platform for studying RNA viruses. The core technique of RNA virus reverse genetics is the generation of viral genomic RNA transcripts within a suitable host cell. Currently, the major recombineering strategies consist of bacterial artificial chromosome (BAC), vaccinia virus vectors and completely plasmid-based reverse genetics systems (Table 1).Table 1RNA viruses rescued using different reverse genetics systems.Table 1MethodVirusPromoterTransfected cellsReporter geneReferencesBACRSV A2-line19FT7BSR-T7/51red fluorescent protein monomeric Katushka 2, Renilla luciferase(Hotard et al., 2012)Vaccinia virus vectorsHCoV 229ET7MRC-52N.A.(Thiel et al., 2001)SARS-CoV HKU-39,849T7BHK-213Renilla luciferase(van den Worm et al., 2012)IBVT7CK4N.A.(Bickerton et al., 2017)Entirely plasmid based reverse genetics systemIAV A/WSN/33, A/PR/8/34pol IHEK293T5N.A.(Neumann et al., 1999)IAV A/WSN/33pol IVeroN.A.(Fodor et al., 1999)GVII NDVpol IIBHK-21green fluorescent protein(Wang et al., 2015)Reovirus T3DT7L9296green fluorescent protein(Kobayashi et al., 2007)Reovirus T3DT7L929, BHK-21, A5497N.A.(Komoto et al., 2014)AHSV-4T7BSR, L929N.A.(Conradie et al., 2016)simian RV strain SA11T7BHK-T78NanoLuc luciferase(Kanai et al., 2017)human RV strain OdeliaT7BHK-T7the reporter-NSP1 chimeric gene from strain SA11(Kawagishi et al., 2020)1BSR-T7/5: Baby hamster kidney cells constitutively expressing the T7 polymerase.2MRC-5: Human lung fibroblast cells.3BHK-21: Baby hamster kidney fibroblast cells.4CK: Chick kidney cells.5HEK293T: Human embryonic kidney cells.6L929: Murine L929 fibroblast cells.7A549: Human lung cancer cells.8BHK-T7: Baby hamster kidney cells constitutively expressing T7pol.2.1Bacterial artificial chromosomeBAC is a strategy by inserting a DNA fragment into a single-copy F plasmid that is stably inherited in E. coli, followed by applying a promoter for transcription. Recovery of the infectious virus is subsequently accomplished by transfecting the purified BAC DNA into appropriate cell lines (Fig. 2A). In 1997, murine cytomegalovirus (MCMV) developed the first viral BAC system, one of the largest herpesviruses with a genome size of 230 kbp (Messerle et al., 1997). For many years, BAC structures have been used to recover large DNA viruses. In 2012, for the first time, the combination of BAC recombination-mediated mutations and negative-stranded RNA virus reverse genetics was achieved. A BAC-based respiratory syncytial virus rescue system was successfully established to recover recombinant virus by direct transfection of mammalian cells (Hotard et al., 2012). In a recent study, a reverse genetics system was constructed for the first time to generate a recombinant virus using a BAC-based torovirus rescue system (Ujike et al., 2022). In addition, BAC enable to combine with CRISPR/Cas9 technology for generation of precise genetic mutations in cells and animal models (Fang et al., 2021a).Fig. 2Schematic of three different strategies for reverse genetic systems. (A) The viral genomic fragment to be rescued is inserted into a BAC plasmid, and infectious cloning is accomplished under promoter control. (B) Cloning of full-length viral cDNA using vaccine virus as a vector. (C) Transfection of cDNA gene-segments into appropriate cell lines relying only on plasmids without helper viruses. After transfection, the virus was cultured, amplified, lysed, and eventually successfully rescued.Fig. 2There are several advantages for BAC vectors. BAC vectors not only facilitate the manipulation of large DNA sequences but can also site-specifically shuttle into E. coli using well-established mutagenesis techniques. High-copy vectors may contain viral sequences that are unstable or toxic to the host to some degree, while BAC tackles this problem as a promising approach capable of using single or low-copy vectors. BAC vectors provide powerful tools for viral detection and antiviral drug screening through the insertion of reporter genes (Hotard et al., 2012; Nguyen et al., 2021). Of note, a limitation of BAC cloning is the requirement of helper viruses or additional expression vectors to obtain recombinant viruses in some cases.2.2Vaccinia virus vectorsReconstruction of the recombinant virus was accomplished by using the vaccinia virus as a vector for cloning, isolating and purifying infectious in vitro RNA transcripts from the recombinant vaccinia virus, following transfection of the RNA transcripts into allowed cell lines (Fig. 2B). In 2001, a full-length cDNA copy of human coronavirus was cloned and propagated in the vaccinia virus genome, and infectious RNA transcripts were generated from this template, culminating in the successful rescue of human coronavirus (Thiel et al., 2001). The emergence of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus (SARS-CoV) in 2002 caused unprecedented nosocomial outbreaks. To combat the disease, a vaccinia virus-based reverse genetic system for SARS-CoV was developed and used to produce a recombinant virus expressing a reporter gene (Renilla luciferase) for the investigation of SARS-CoV pathogenesis (van den Worm et al., 2012).The superiority of vaccinia virus is its genome that contains a wide range of non-essential regions for replication and allows the insertion of large segments of exogenous genes without loss of integrity, stability and infectivity. Secondly, the cloned cDNA inserts can be used to mediate homologous recombination by the vaccinia virus and to restore cDNAs with erroneous nucleotide changes caused by RT-PCR. Unfortunately, the vaccinia virus vector also suffers from inefficiency. The rescued virus still undergoes complex and time-consuming steps to get isolated from the vaccinia virus and may cause adverse effects on virus replication, which hampered the application of this system.2.3Entirely plasmid-based reverse genetics systemA plasmid-based reverse genetics system does not rely on helper viruses. This system only transfects plasmids containing cDNA sequences into appropriate cell lines and directly drives the transcription and replication of infectious cDNA clones within the cells, ultimately resulting in infectious daughter viruses (Fig. 2C). This system was first implemented for influenza viruses. In 1999, a recombinant influenza A virus (IAV) was rescued entirely from cDNA, driven by RNA polymerase I (pol I), in the absence of any helper virus (Fodor et al., 1999; Neumann et al., 1999). Based on this research, plasmid-only reverse genetic systems continue to be implemented in various virus rescues.In addition to utilizing pol I/II drivers, reverse genetic systems targeting reovirus commonly use the T7 RNA polymerase promoter. In 2007, an entirely plasmid-based reverse genetics system for mammalian reovirus was developed to generate infectious viruses from cloned cDNA (Kobayashi et al., 2007). With less than a decade, the process of rescuing reovirus has become simple to design. A rescue system consisting of a plasmid-encoded T7 RNA polymerase lessens its reliance on T7pol-expressing cells and theoretically provides the possibility to produce reovirus in any cell line (Komoto et al., 2014). Unfortunately, this attempt did not overcome the problem of low recovery efficiency albeit it greatly improved the flexibility of reovirus reverse genetic system. Previous reports have suggested that higher virus recovery may be obtained by improving transfection efficiency and optimizing the ratio of transfected plasmids (Kobayashi et al., 2010). Therefore, the African horse sickness virus (AHSV) reverse genetic system was simplified evaluated and expanded on this principle. AHSV-based reverse genetic system incorporates the T7 RNA polymerase into one of the plasmids and reduces plasmid quantity to improve the viral recovery (Conradie et al., 2016). In addition to this, an entirely plasmid-based reverse genetic system has been used to rescue rotavirus (RV) and to investigate the role of its nonstructural protein NSP1 in viral replication and in disrupting the host innate immune response (Kanai et al., 2017; Kawagishi et al., 2020).The major advantage of the entirely plasmid-based reverse genetic system is that it does not rely on helper viruses and therefore eliminates possible interference from heterologous viruses on viral replication and transcription. Since the viral genome is transcribed directly in the cell to ensure the quality of RNA transcription, RNA degradation can be avoided and obtained RNA transcripts that are relatively stable and infectious. The pol I/II promoter rescue system is simple to operate and has the advantages of corrective function, wide cellular adaptability, and no need for prolonged in vitro manipulation, but its transcriptional capacity is limited, transcripts are at risk of being sheared, and virus rescue efficiency is not high. In parallel, the rescue system using the T7 promoter is being optimized. Using the plasmid encoded T7 RNA polymerase, time-consuming screening tests for the selection of animal target cell lines which express stable T7 RNA polymerase can be avoided. In addition, the ability to recover mutated and recombined viruses suggest that the system could be used to generate further recombined viruses, and these viruses with any desired combination of gene fragments could be potential live attenuated vaccines.3Current status of reverse genetic research on norovirus3.1Reverse genetics of norovirus and Caliciviridae family3.1.1Human norovirusRescue human norovirus was first used a vaccinia virus encoding T7 RNA polymerase to express human norovirus GI.1 genome in mammalian cells and packaged its RNA into viral particles (Asanaka et al., 2005). Subsequently, an entirely plasmid-based reverse genetics system for human norovirus GII.3 strain was established driven by a mammalian elongation factor-1α (EF-1α) promoter, which was highly versatile and had broad applicability to other noroviruses. This system enabled to produce infectious progeny virions in multiple cell lines, with the highest viral yield in African green monkey kidney (COS7) cells up to 8.0 × 104 copies per 106 cells (Katayama et al., 2014). In addition, CMV-driven GII.4 Sydney cDNA was cloned and inserted into the replication subsystem of the green fluorescent protein (GFP) reporter gene. The replicon containing GFP was then transfected into human lung cancer (Caco-2) cells and expressed viral structural proteins (Oliveira et al., 2018).3.1.2Murine norovirusVaccinia virus caused cytopathy and negatively affected murine norovirus replication, thereby switching to fowlpox virus for restoration of infectious murine norovirus. Murine norovirus transcript was then transfected into BHK-21 cells with typical yields approaching to 5 × 104 TCID50 per 35 mm dish and BSR-T7 cells with 1 × 104 TCID50/mL (Chaudhry et al., 2007; Arias et al., 2012b). Murine norovirus can also be recovered by driving cDNA expression in human hepatocellular carcinoma cell line G2 (HepG2) cells and HEK293T cells using pol II as a promoter, but the viral titers obtained by this method were much lower than those acquired using fowlpox virus (Ward et al., 2007). Besides these strategies, norovirus reverse genetics can be achieved by in vitro transcription with T7 RNA polymerase. This approach relied on optimizing the in vitro RNA addition cap and murine macrophage cell line (RAW 264.7) electroporation conditions and provided the robust recovery of murine norovirus yield of up to 109 TCID50 per 6 × 106 cells (Yunus et al., 2010).3.1.3Caliciviridae familyIn addition to norovirus, reverse genetics systems of other viruses in the Caliciviridae family have been successfully established as well. The full-length cDNA clones synthesized with capped RNA were transcribed in vitro using T7 RNA polymerase as a promoter and transfected with Crandell-Rees feline kidney (CRFK) cells to obtain infectious feline calicivirus (FCV), and the cleavage role of proteases was clarified by site-directed mutagenesis of the capsid precursor cleavage site (Sosnovtsev et al., 1998). FCV was rescued by transfection of recombinant plasmids containing the viral genome and the EMCV IRES sequence placed upstream of it into BHK-21 and HEK293T cells expressing T7 RNA polymerase (Sandoval-Jaime et al., 2015). And the sapoviruses (both porcine sapovirus and human sapovirus) could be also recovered using the T7 RNA polymerase in vitro transcription system with a capping of the 5′ end (Lu et al., 2016; Li et al., 2022).3.2Viral genome structure and protein functionReverse genetics systems are powerful tools to propagate noroviruses in vitro and are widely applied to evaluate genome structures, protein functions, pathogenesis and antiviral therapies of different noroviruses (Table 2).Table 2Application of reverse genetics systems in norovirus-related studies.Table 2Application AreasVirusGenome ManipulationFindingsReferencesViral Genome Structure and Protein FunctionMurine NorovirusIntroduction of substitutions in the 5′ end (SL8, SL29), sgRNA (SLa5045) and 3′ end (SL7330) to generate mutantsDisruption of the 5′ end stem-loops reduced infectivity by 15 to 20-fold, but disruption of the RNA structure in the sg promoter region and at the 3′ end resulted in replication loss.(Simmonds et al., 2008)Murine Norovirus-1.
