Serial sections of these samples were stained with anti–IL-1α and detected with DAB as illustrated in the middle and right panels (magnification, 630×). IL-1α expression was analyzed in cells expressing VZV proteins as shown within the area outlined in the left panel and in neighboring uninfected epidermal cells in the same section. IL-1α was activated and translocated to the nuclei of VZV infected cells (middle) but showed a diffuse cytoplasmic stain in neighboring uninfected cells (right).Like IL-α, IFN-α was expressed constitutively in uninfected skin cells. In VZV-infected skin xenografts, IFN-α was down-regulated consistently within VZV infected cells, whereas it was expressed prominently in neighboring uninfected epidermal cells (Fig. 3 A). Phosphorylation of Stat 1 protein was examined to confirm this evidence of inhibition of the IFN-α pathway in VZV-infected cells and its activation in uninfected cells. IFN-α ligation to IFN-α receptors induces tyrosine phosphorylation of Stat1 by JAK kinases (8). IFN-α is inhibited if Stat1 does not undergo phosphorylation and nuclear translocation. Nuclear, phosphorylated Stat1 was detected in uninfected epidermal cells near VZV-infected cells but not in cells expressing VZV proteins (Fig. 3 B). Although IFN-α was expressed constitutively, Stat1 was not phosphorylated and remained cytoplasmic in uninfected skin xenografts (Fig. 3 B). These observations indicated that a VZV gene product(s) blocks Stat1 activation in order to inhibit IFN-α production in foci of infected skin cells in vivo.Figure 3.IFN-α expression and Stat1 phosphorylation in VZV-infected and uninfected epidermal cells. Formalin- fixed, paraffin-embedded sections of VZV-infected skin xenografts were pretreated and double stained with anti-VZV IgG, detected with DAB (brown), and anti–IFN-α or anti-pStat1 antibody detected with Vector VIP (purple). Sections are shown at magnification 200×. (A) Infected cells were identified by VZV protein (brown) expression. In double labeled skin sections, IFN-α (purple) expression was prominent in adjacent uninfected cells but not in VZV-infected cells (top) compared with sections stained with rabbit IgG as a control for IFN-α (bottom). (B) In double labeled sections, phosphorylated Stat1 (purple) was up-regulated in adjacent uninfected cells but absent in VZV-infected cells (top); pStat1 was not detected in uninfected skin (bottom right) compared with rabbit IgG control stain (bottom left).Inhibition of Type I IFN Signaling.To document the relevance of these observations about IFN-α and Stat1 phosphorylation to VZV pathogenesis, skin xenografts in five mice (n = 10 xenografts) were inoculated with VZV and mice were given neutralizing antibody against the IFN-α/β receptor, which blocks type I IFN activity (9). Four skin xenografts were harvested from mice in the antibody-treated and control groups 7 d after VZV inoculation for viral titrations. The titer of infectious VZV was 10-fold higher in skin from antibody-treated animals (Fig. 4 E). VZV was recovered from all xenografts from mice given anti–IFN-α/β receptor antibody compared with three of four xenografts from controls. In the other xenografts examined by immunohistochemistry, diminished IFN signaling was shown to result in substantially larger cutaneous lesions (Fig. 4, C and D). Stat1 was activated and localized to nuclei of neighboring uninfected cells in control animals (Fig. 4 A). Phosphorylated Stat1 was detected in some cells, primarily at the margins of VZV lesions, in mice given anti–IFN-α/β receptor (Fig. 4 B).Figure 4.Blocking of IFN-α signaling enhanced VZV replication in skin. Skin xenografts were infected with VZV by direct inoculation in mice treated with anti-IFNα/βRβ antibody or controls and harvested at day 7 after infection. Half of the skin implant was fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for histological analysis, and the other half was disassociated into cell suspension to measure virus titers by infectious focus assay. (A and B) Shown are representative results from skin sections examined at 7 d (large arrow, VZV lesion); phosphorylated Stat1 (purple; small arrow) was translocated to nuclei in adjacent cells but not within VZV lesions (magnification, 200×). (C and D) Skin lesions shown by staining with anti-VZV IgG (purple) were larger at day 7 in animals given anti-IFNα/βRβ antibody (right) than controls (left) (magnification, 100×). (E) Mean VZV titers in four skin xenografts from two mice were 10-fold higher in anti-IFNα/βRβ antibody-treated animals compared with controls (P < 0.05, unpaired t test).Migration of Mononuclear Cells into VZV-infected Skin.In these experiments, one of two bilateral skin xenografts was inoculated with VZV-infected HEL cells and the other with uninfected fibroblasts. 10 d later, uninfected mononuclear cells were injected i.v., and skin xenografts were harvested after 24–48 h. Mononuclear cells within VZV-infected skin xenografts expressed CD3, whereas no CD20+ B cells were detected in three experiments (Table II). CD4+ and CD8+ T cells were distributed uniformly with no evidence of increased numbers near VZV lesions. Infiltrating cells were exclusively CD45RO+ T cells (Table II). T cells expressing CLA were detected at low frequencies (<1%), but CCR4+ T cells were not identified. Total numbers of T cells recovered from VZV-infected skin were slightly higher than corresponding uninfected xenografts, but surface marker profiles were comparable by flow cytometry. The relative percentages of subpopulations were as observed when uninfected mononuclear cells were transferred (Table I). Thus, T cell migration into skin was not influenced by VZV protein expression or cellular proteins, IL-1α or IFN-α, in the absence of other signals.The analysis of lesion biopsies from VZV-infected patients showed many infiltrating mononuclear cells, most of which expressed CD4 or CD8; a few CD20+ B cells and IFN-α–expressing cells, probably macrophages, were also detected (Table II). CD45RO+ memory T cells, naive CD45RA+ T cells, and CLA+ and CCR4+ T cells were present in comparable numbers (Table II). The differences in cell profiles between VZV lesion biopsies and VZV-infected skin xenografts after adoptive transfer suggested that recruitment and/or retention of skin homing T cells, naïve T cells, B cells, and macrophages required host immune-mediated signals.Expression of Endothelial Cell Adhesion Molecules.Since skin homing of memory T cells is regulated by adhesion molecules and chemoattractant receptors (10), adhesion molecule expression was examined to explain differences between T cell subpopulations detected in biopsies of VZV lesions and VZV-infected skin xenografts. Expression of E-selectin, ICAM-1, or VCAM-1 by endothelial cells was not detected in VZV-infected skin xenografts, indicating that VZV replication, which is associated with the expression of all kinetic classes of viral proteins, and altered IL-1α and IFN-α expression alone did not induce adhesion molecules (Fig. 5, left). In contrast, all adhesion molecules were expressed extensively in VZV lesion biopsies when host cellular immunity was intact (Fig. 5, right).Figure 5.Expression of adhesion molecules by cutaneous endothelial cells in VZV-infected skin xenografts and biopsies of VZV skin lesions. Serial frozen sections of VZV-infected skin xenografts (left) or lesion biopsies from patients with varicella or herpes zoster (right) were stained with antibodies against adhesion molecules expressed by endothelial cells. Signals were detected with Vector VIP (purple) and counterstained with methyl green. Representative results from one of three VZV-infected skin xenografts and one of five VZV lesion biopsies are shown for expression of CD31, E-selectin, ICAM-1, and VCAM-1. E-selectin, ICAM-1, and VCAM-1 were highly expressed by CD31-positive dermal endothelial cells in patient lesion biopsies but were not detected in VZV infected skin xenografts (asterisk, VZV skin lesion). Magnification, 100×.DiscussionAlthough the signs and symptoms of infections caused by human herpesviruses are well documented, much less is known about critical events in pathogenesis that precede the onset of the clinical illness. These experiments using the SCIDhu mouse model of VZV pathogenesis provide evidence that infectious VZV can be transferred by T cells through the circulation to sites of replication in skin, resulting in the formation of typical cutaneous lesions. The observations suggest that VZV tropism for T cells, which has been shown in vitro and in T cell xenografts in SCIDhu mice, contributes to the pathogenesis of primary VZV infection in vivo (3–5). The adoptive transfer of uninfected and VZV-infected human mononuclear cells was associated with enrichment of memory CD4+ T cells within human skin xenografts in the SCIDhu mouse model. Therefore, we suggest that VZV tropism for T cells permits the virus to take advantage of the usual pathways for T cell migration through skin during immune surveillance. Whereas naïve T cells enter LNs through the high endothelial venules, exit through efferent lymphatics, and return to the blood, memory T cells traffic through skin and other tissues. In our experiments, the percentage of naïve CD4+ T cells recovered from skin xenografts was only 0.7–3% compared with ∼30% in the infused population. In previous work, we reported that VZV preferentially infects memory T cells compared with naïve CD4+ T cells at a ratio of 3:1 in vitro (5). Lymphoid tissues of the upper respiratory tract, including tonsils and adenoids, contain activated, memory T cells, which may become infected when VZV infects respiratory mucosa. Together, these observations suggest that two factors, which are the intrinsic propensity of memory CD4+ T cells to migrate into skin tissue and the enhanced susceptibility of memory CD4+ T cells to VZV infection, may combine to create an important role for memory CD4+ T cells in VZV pathogenesis. Thus, memory CD4+ T cells that become infected at sites of respiratory epithelial inoculation may be more likely to deliver VZV to epidermal cells and initiate the cutaneous phase of infection than other circulating cells of the immune system, such as naïve CD4+ T cells. As a clinical correlate, VZV dissemination to skin may be modulated in young children, who have few memory T cells, whereas adults with varicella who have >75% memory CD4+ T cells usually develop many cutaneous lesions (1).Memory T cells that express CLA or CCR4 are targeted to skin through interactions with adhesion molecules and chemoattracts when inflammation is triggered (11). We detected a two- to fivefold enrichment of CLA+ CD4+ T cells in skin when SCIDhu mice were given uninfected human mononuclear cells, but the percentage remained ≤3.6 of CD4+ T cells. We did not demonstrate any increase in the numbers of CLA+ or CCR4+ CD4 T cells in skin after the adoptive transfer of VZV-infected T cells. These observations suggest that VZV pathogenesis does not depend on a selective infection of memory CD4+ T cell subpopulations that express specific skin homing markers. Since the epidermis should be in its resting state during the initial transfer of VZV to skin by infected T cells, trafficking of CLA+ or CCR4+ T cells should not be selectively involved in the initial phase of VZV pathogenesis. A second clinical correlate is that skin trauma, such as sunburn acquired during the incubation period, is associated with a much more severe varicella rash. Under such conditions, the twofold increase in infectivity of VZV for CLA+ T cells that we observed in vitro, combined with the increased migration of these cells to damaged skin, could facilitate more efficient transfer of VZV to the epidermis. The down-regulation of MHC class I molecules that we have observed on VZV-infected T cells may also contribute to successful VZV transport to skin (12).VZV transmission to other susceptible individuals requires enough replication to create lesions that contain infectious virus at the skin surface (Fig. 6). However, cell–cell spread in vivo at the rate characteristic of VZV replication in human fibroblasts in vitro would be life threatening to the host and would therefore diminish opportunities for person-to-person transmission. Examining VZV lesion formation in parallel with innate antiviral responses in skin xenografts in vivo showed IFN-α down-regulation in VZV-infected cells and no induction of adhesion molecules on capillary endothelial cells. These conditions favor the pathogen during the early phase of skin infection. At the same time, IFN-α production by epidermal cells adjacent to VZV-infected cells appears to provide an innate barrier against aggressive spread of VZV from cell to cell in skin.Figure 6.A model of the pathogenesis of primary VZV infection. T cells within the local lymphoid tissue of the respiratory tract may become infected by transfer of VZV from its initial site of inoculation in respiratory epithelial cells. T cells may then transport the virus to the skin immediately and release infectious VZV. The remainder of the 10–21-d incubation period appears to be the interval required for VZV to overcome the innate IFN-α response in enough epidermal cells to create the typical vesicular lesions containing cell-free virus at the skin surface. The signaling of enhanced IFN-α production in adjacent skin cells may prevent a rapid, uncontrolled cell–cell spread of VZV. Secondary “crops” of varicella lesions may result when T cells traffic through early stage cutaneous lesions become infected and produce a secondary viremia. Intact host immune responses appear to be required to trigger up-regulation of adhesion molecules, facilitating the clearance of VZV by adaptive immunity.Our analysis of IFN-α and IL-1α in VZV-infected and uninfected skin xenografts revealed a subtle interaction between VZV and epidermal cell cytokine responses. Type I interferons, IFN-α, and to a lesser extent, IFN-β, are the predominant mediators of innate antiviral activity. Constitutive IFN-α/β expression occurs in some cells or tissues, allowing an immediate antiviral response (13). IFN-α/β activation is induced by the Jak/Stat pathway when ligands bind to IFN-α/β receptors and stimulate transcription of the IFN regulatory factors (IRFs) (8). IRF3 and IRF7 are crucial for maximal expression of IFN-α/β (14, 15). Constitutive IFN-α/β signaling is thought to sustain IRF7 expression and enhance IFN-α/β production in a positive feedback loop in response to viral infection (16). Most viruses have mechanisms to inhibit synthesis of IFNs or evade downstream antiviral effects in order to allow viral spread before adaptive immunity develops. HSV, a human alphaherpesvirus closely related to VZV, has several such mechanisms (17).We found that IFN-α was expressed constitutively in the epidermis, independently of Stat1 activation in uninfected skin xenografts. After VZV infection, IFN-α expression was down-regulated in VZV-infected cells concurrently with inhibition of Stat1 phosphorylation. In contrast, Stat1 was phosphorylated and translocated to nuclei, accompanied by IFN-α up-regulation in neighboring, uninfected cells. The capacity of VZV to block IFN-α in some cells enables the virus to replicate, spread from cell to cell, and create focal cutaneous lesions, whereas IFN-α activation protects the adjacent cells. Blocking the IFN-α/β receptor enhanced VZV replication and lesion formation in vivo, showing that these patterns of IFN-α expression and Jak/Stat signaling have biological importance for regulating VZV pathogenesis. Experiments are in progress to identify VZV proteins that have the capacity to disrupt the IFN-α pathway. Overall, the innate IFN-α response appears to modulate VZV growth, providing a substantial barrier against cell–cell spread in skin during the prolonged varicella incubation period. Our observations suggest that VZV gradually overcomes this barrier in order to form polykaryocytes, eventually creating a vesicular lesion that penetrates the skin surface (Fig. 6).IL-1α is synthesized constitutively and stored in suprabasal layers of the epidermis as a 31-kD precursor molecule, pre–IL-1α (18, 19). When cells die, pre–IL-1α is released and cleaved into a 17-kD IL-1α molecule by extracellular proteases. IL-1α can also be released by the calcium-dependent cysteine proteases called calpains, which are ubiquitously but weakly expressed in all cell types (20). Mature IL-1α displaces the IL-1 receptor antagonist and binds to IL-1αR. Internalization and accumulation of the IL-1α–IL-1 receptor complex in the nucleus induces genes involved in skin cell proliferation and other inflammatory changes (21, 22). We found that IL-1α was expressed constitutively in skin but remained in the cytoplasm of uninfected cells adjacent to and distant from VZV lesions. In contrast, IL-1α accumulated in nuclei of VZV-infected cells. This pattern suggests that IL-1α is activated directly or indirectly by VZV replication within epidermal cells. However, IL-1α is apparently not released, or its release into the local skin microenvironment fails to trigger IL-1α activation or enhanced IL-1α production by neighboring cells.Expression of cellular adhesion molecules on endothelial cells increases the efficiency of T cell trafficking. Their expression can be regulated by inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1α, TNF-α, and IFN-γ, which were produced by cells infected with some viral pathogens (23–26). In our experiments, VZV-infected T cells migrated into skin and released infectious virus for entry into and replication in epidermal and dermal cells without preexisting expression of E-selectin, ICAM-1, or VCAM-1 on endothelial cells, and without eliciting the expression of these inflammatory proteins. Although IL-1α was activated in VZV-infected cells, it remained cytoplasmic in uninfected cells and did not have the capacity to induce adhesion molecules on endothelial cells in skin xenografts. VZV replication did not induce TNF-α production by skin cells. In contrast, widespread expression of E-selectin, ICAM-1, and VCAM-1 by endothelial cells was observed in biopsies of clinical VZV lesions. CLA+ T cells were enriched in lesion biopsies compared with VZV-infected skin xenografts, which is consistent with a requirement for host immune mechanisms to up-regulate adhesion molecules. This comparative analysis indicated that endothelial cell activation was not stimulated by VZV gene products alone, despite their extensive expression during lytic infection of epidermal and dermal cells, but required host immune mechanisms.Infectious VZV can be recovered from peripheral blood mononuclear cells during the last few days of the incubation period of varicella in the healthy host and for 2–3 d after the rash appears. We speculate that this secondary viremia results from infection of migrating T cells by virus produced in lesions that are not yet visible at the skin surface (Fig. 6). This hypothesis is suggested by our finding that many T cells entered VZV-infected skin xenografts after adoptive transfer. Thus, viral amplification could result from progressive VZV infection in skin without requiring a phase of replication in reticuloendothelial tissues during the incubation period. Our experiments do not exclude some VZV replication in liver or other reticuloendothelial organs, which might contribute to pathogenesis by increasing the viral load. However, our data indicate that the interval required for VZV to overcome innate immune barriers in skin is sufficient to account for the prolonged incubation period. Continued VZV replication in skin would also be predicted to sustain the viremia associated with malignant varicella, which leads to pneumonia, hepatitis, and encephalitis in immunocompromised children who fail to develop VZV-specific adaptive immunity (1). Further, the transfer of VZV from infected epidermal cells into migratory T cells may also explain how VZV causes viremia and dissemination in high-risk patients with herpes zoster.Based on these SCIDhu mouse experiments, we offer a new paradigm of primary VZV infection which suggests new directions for the analysis of events in VZV pathogenesis. According to this model, infectious VZV is transferred to skin shortly after inoculation of the respiratory mucosa. Although other cell types may be involved, memory CD4+ T cells play a prominent role in this process because of their intrinsic pattern of skin trafficking and their increased susceptibility to VZV infection. VZV gene products modulate innate epidermal cell defenses, down-regulating IFN-α to ensure localized replication in skin. Epidermal cell infection appears to occur without activating endothelial cell adhesion molecules, thereby delaying the invasion of antiviral inflammatory cells at the early stage of cutaneous lesion formation. At the same time, uninfected epidermal cells are signaled to mount a potent innate IFN-α response, which counters an overly aggressive cell–cell spread in skin (Fig. 6). This model helps to explain how VZV replication may be restricted by the host even though VZV-specific T cell immunity is not detected until after the appearance of vesicular skin lesions (1). Acquisition of T cells that recognize VZV proteins correlates with cessation of skin replication, which we suggest is necessary to stop continued, secondary T cell viremia. A benign infectious process during the initial phase of VZV pathogenesis and a circumscribed clinical illness provides the optimal strategy for VZV to be sustained within the human population (27).


Title: The live attenuated varicella-zoster virus vaccine vOka: Molecular and cellular biology of its skin attenuation

IntroductionVaricella-zoster virus (VZV) is a human alphaherpesvirus. Infection with VZV causes chickenpox (varicella) and, upon reactivation from latency, herpes zoster (HZ), also known as shingles.1 In immunocompetent individuals, chickenpox manifests as a generalized skin blistering rash, whereas HZ is accompanied by a painful blistering rash, limited to the region of the skin innervated by the sensory ganglion from which latent virus has reactivated.1VZV transmission to naïve hosts occurs through contact with skin lesions and/or inhalation of the aerosolised infectious cell-free virus, which is shed by the skin blisters or, to a lesser extent, by the upper respiratory tract mucosa. Transmitted virus is inhaled by susceptible contacts, resulting in infection of the upper respiratory tract epithelia. Transportation of virus by epithelial dendritic cells (DCs), to lymphoid organs leads to uptake by skin-homing T lymphocytes, which traffic the virus to skin.2,3 There, the virus appears to initially infect cells of the hair follicles (HFs) and the keratinocytes which populate the basal immature layer of the epidermis.4–6 VZV replicates in the epidermal keratinocytes and this process culminates with the formation of cutaneous blisters, which are laden with infectious cell-free virus. The formation of cell-free virus in cutaneous blisters is critical to VZV transmission to new hosts, as well as for establishment of latency; cell-free virus, which is only present in blisters, is required for establishment of latency in sensory ganglia through infection of sensory nerve endings in the skin and retrograde spread.7,8Although in immunocompetent children chickenpox is usually self-limiting, this may not be the case for immunocompromised individuals or even healthy adults, where chickenpox may cause severe complications, including as a result of bacterial superinfections. HZ is also potentially debilitating, with postherpetic neuralgia (PHN), which manifests as prolonged pain, continuing for months after rash presentation. PHN occurs in about 15% of HZ cases.9 Both HZ and PHN occur more frequently later in life and are associated with declining cell-mediated immunity (CMI).9,10 HZ is also more common in immunocompromised populations including those with HIV, transplant recipients and others with reduced CMI.9,11In 1974, Takahashi and colleagues12 developed the live attenuated vOka-strain vaccine, for prevention of varicella. In those countries that have adopted routine vaccination since, the incidence of chickenpox has highly declined, and several post-licensing studies have confirmed the vaccine’s efficacy, as well as its safety.9,13,14 A therapeutic vaccine for HZ has also been developed, which contains higher concentration of the vOka virus.15 More recently, an adjuvanted HZ subunit vaccine based on the VZV glycoprotein gE has been developed.16 Because the vOka vaccine is based on live attenuated VZV virus, concerns were initially raised about its safety in the long term if the vaccine virus became latent and could then reactivate to cause HZ. However, it was demonstrated that, even though it can establish latency in sensory nerves, vOka rarely reactivates causing HZ (reactivation occurs at least seven times less frequently).14,17,18 The vOka vaccine can also cause rashes, but this occurs less frequently (less than 5% of cases) and where it does happen, there are few lesions.18 Transmission of the vaccine virus to susceptible hosts is also much more infrequent than with wild-type VZV.13Sequencing analyses of the vOka vaccine preparations have shown them to be genetically highly heterogenous with multiple mutations, mostly occurring at low frequency. Fixed vaccine mutations have consistently been observed in some key genes like the major VZV transcriptional transactivator ORF62 and ORF0.19–21 However, the functional implications of these mutations are still poorly understood. The vOka strain replicates significantly less efficiently than wild-type VZV in keratinocytes and skin tissues,22,23 but similarly to wild-type in T lymphocytes or neurons.2,24 Reduced vOka epithelial replication with less cell-free virus results in the clinically attenuated vOka phenotype with interrupted transmission and establishment of latency while maintaining immunological priming. Nevertheless, the exact molecular and cellular mechanisms behind vOka skin attenuation remain largely unknown. The aim of this review is to gather the existing evidence on the epithelial signaling and other pathways that are altered by the vOka virus, compared to wild-type VZV and highlight gaps in existing knowledge. To this end, the review will provide an overview of what is currently known about the molecular biology of the vOka vaccine, its genetic heterogeneity and how this may influence the way vOka interacts with host skin pathways with which wild-type VZV is known to interconnect, thereby exposing possible mechanisms of skin attenuation.History of the vOka vaccineThe first vaccine against varicella was developed in 1974 at the University of Osaka, Japan, by Takahashi and colleagues, with the aim of protecting children at high risk of developing severe complications from the disease. A VZV strain was isolated from an infected child, the so-called parental Oka strain (pOka), named after the patient. This strain was attenuated in vitro using the traditional method of passaging the virus multiple times at varying temperatures (including low temperatures to which the wild-type virus is not adapted) and in different cell lines (including non-human cells). Specifically, the isolate was passaged 11 times in human embryonic lung cells, followed by 12 passages in guinea pig embryonic fibroblasts and a few more passages in human diploid cells (WI-38).12 This attenuation procedure resulted in the vaccine Oka strain (vOka).Early clinical trials were conducted in Japan and included healthy and sick or immunocompromised children.12,25 Notably, in the very first study using vOka, the vaccine was administered to 23 hospitalized and seronegative children in contact with a child manifesting varicella symptoms.12 All the vaccinated children seroconverted, including those on immunosuppressive steroid regimens. Similarly, in a follow-up study, vaccination of 11 children before or following a case of varicella in a children’s hospital ward prevented the spread of the infection to other susceptible children.25 Early studies in Japan also included household contacts that had no history of varicella and were seronegative.26 Collectively, these initial studies showed that the live attenuated vaccine was effective in inducing an immunological response in all vaccinees, without any significant clinical reactions in either healthy or high-risk individuals. Follow-up studies, up to 2 y after administration of the vaccine in Japan, confirmed the development of immunity against varicella in both healthy and immunocompromised children.27Further clinical trials were carried out in subsequent years, mainly in the US. In 1984, Wiebel et al. demonstrated in the first in-kind USA study that vaccination using the live attenuated vOka vaccine protects healthy children from varicella.28 Later that year, a study demonstrated the vaccine’s safety and efficiency in preventing the emergence of severe varicella symptoms in children suffering from leukemia.29 Despite multiple studies exhibiting its high safety and efficacy, the vOka vaccine was met with concern that the latent virus could potentially be harmful in the long term.9 The first countries to license the use of the live attenuated vaccine were Germany and Sweden in 1984,30 followed by Korea and Japan in 1988.31 In 1995, the live attenuated vaccine was licensed in the USA,31 where carefully conducted post-licensing surveillance studies have shown a drop in the incidence of varicella, as well as hospitalizations due to the infection.32,33 Follow-up of vaccinees for up to 7 y post-vaccination shows efficacy levels of up to 94.4% after a single dose and 98.3% after two doses of the vaccine.34 There is an ongoing debate regarding the optimal vaccination program, and whether one or two doses of the vaccine should be administered. One-dose vaccinations are proven to be highly effective in preventing severe varicella. At the same time, with one-dose vaccination, sufficient circulating varicella is maintained to boost immunity in both vaccinees and naturally infected individuals. This is important because, according to the model of HZ pathogenesis first illustrated by Hope-Simpson,10 CMI to VZV is boosted either by endogenous exposure to VZV through silent reactivation of the virus or by exogenous exposure to the virus, through the contact with a case of varicella. Notwithstanding, higher antibody count and seroconversion rates have been reported for individuals receiving two doses of the vaccine (with the second dose administered 3 months after the first) with fewer breakthrough infections35,36 and this led the USA to a shift toward two-dose vaccination in 2007.37Currently, the licensed, commercially available vaccines against varicella, which are based on the live attenuated vOka strain include VarilRix® (GSK), VariVax® (Merck), OkaVax® (Biken), and Baike® (Chanchung Biotechnology). A combined vaccine against measles, mumps, rubella and varicella (MMRV) is also licensed and distributed by Merck (ProQuad®) or GSK (Priorix-Tetra®).Apart from vaccines based on the Oka strain, in South Korea, a vaccine based on the MAV/06 strain is distributed by GC Biopharma under the name Barycela® (previously called Suduvax®). SuduVax® was first licensed in 1994. The parental strain was isolated in South Korea from a young child with chickenpox, and like the Oka strain was passaged multiple times in different cell lines (including guinea pig embryonic lung cells) and under different conditions until it was attenuated.38 In 2019, another vaccine was licensed in South Korea; the SKY Varicella® which is distributed by SK Bioscience. This live attenuated vaccine strain is called Oka/SK and is based on yet another VZV isolate. However, the Oka/SK strain appears to be genetically more similar to pOka than to vOka, and to be associated with increased numbers of adverse reactions to the vaccine.39The successful creation of a live attenuated vaccine against varicella laid the foundation for the development of a vaccine against herpes zoster. This vaccine is based on the same vOka strain as the varicella vaccine but contains a much higher concentration of plaque forming units (pfu) per dose (~14 times more). This is a therapeutic and not a prophylactic vaccine because it is administered to individuals who have already been infected with VZV in order to prevent reactivation of the latent virus and the occurrence of HZ and PHN caused by age-associated decrease in the CMI to VZV.9,10,15 The Shingles Prevention Study showed that this zoster vaccine reduces by half the incidence of HZ and by more than 60% the incidence of PHN.15 A subsequent study tested the effectiveness of one dose of the zoster vaccine (which was by then licensed and distributed with the name of Zostavax® from Merck) directed to younger people (50–59 y old) and found that the vaccine had even higher efficacy (69,9% efficacy).40 More recently, a non-live vaccine has been developed for prevention of HZ.16 This is an adjuvanted glycoprotein gE subunit vaccine, called Shingrix® (GSK), which has been shown to be more effective than the live attenuated vaccine Zostavax in preventing HZ and PHN, as well as being indicated for administration to immunocompromised individuals. As a result, in a number of countries, like the USA, the Shingrix vaccine has now largely replaced Zostavax.41The genetics of the vOka vaccine virusThe process of creating the vOka attenuated virus included multiple passaging, sometimes in unnatural conditions (e.g. lower temperatures or unnatural hosts), which lead to accumulation of high number of genetic mutations. The vOka virus consists of a mixture of genotypes bearing several mutations, for example, VariVax vOka contains 292 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs).21,42The comparative analysis of three commercially available VZV vaccines, VariVax (and Zostavax for HZ) from Merck, VarilRix from GSK and OkaVax from Biken, has identified 137 SNPs that are shared between all vaccine preparations.21 Most of the reported mutations are represented with low allele frequencies, except for six, which are fixed or near-fixation (allele frequency > 90%) (Table 1). Of these, five lie in ORF62, which encodes the immediate-early protein IE62, the major VZV transcriptional transactivator.3 Of these five mutations, four have allele frequency > 98%. Two are non-synonymous (NS) (16262 (R958G), 17252 (S628G)) and two synonymous (18111 (P341) and 105,705 (A1143))21 (Figure 1 and Table 1). Notably, the two NS mutations are in the highly conserved regions 2 and 4 of the ORF62 gene. Importantly, these four mutations are also observed in vOka virus retrieved from vaccine-caused skin rashes.20 The sixth near-fixed mutation is located at position 560 of ORF0, which abolishes a stop codon (*130 R) leading to the expression of a variant protein which is 92 amino acids longer.21,43
Figure 1.Schematic of ORF62 gene in the vOka virus. Red vertical lines indicate the four near-fixed mutations with allele frequency >98%. Of these, the dashed lines indicate the two non-synonymous mutations, which both lay in the highly conserved regions 2 and 4 (indicated in blue). The main known functional domains in the IE62 protein and viral or host proteins binding regions are indicated in pink (the provided co-ordinates refer to the VZV Dumas strain). DBD, DNA binding domain; NLS, nuclear localisation signal.Table 1.Allele frequency of near-fixed mutations in the Varivax, VarilRix and Oka/Vax vaccines.NucleotidePositionAmino AcidPositionORFpOkavOkaAmino Acid SubstitutionsMean allele frequency VarivaxMean allele frequency VarilRixAllele frequency Oka/Vax (Biken)5601300TC*130R94.3%98.8%96.2%15544119762AGV1197A93.4%99.5%97.6%15705114362TC 99.5%99.9%100%1626295862TCR958G100%100%100%1725262862TCS628G98.7%100%100%1811134162TC 98.7%100%100%Interestingly, most of these mutations are similarly found in the live attenuated vaccines Baike,44 and Suduvax.38 Intriguingly, three of these mutations (560 in ORF0; 16262 and 107,252 in ORF62) are also found in the VZV high-passage laboratory strain Ellen.43It is important to note that in the rare cases of vaccine breakthrough, the distribution of genotypes in breakthrough infections was similar to the distribution of genotypes circulating at the time, confirming that the vaccine protects equally against all genotypes. Furthermore, there is no evidence of an association of particular SNPs with more severe disease.20,45To understand whether this vast accumulation of mutations in vOka may be caused by the extensive virus passaging performed to develop the vaccine, Kim et al.46 passaged two VZV strains, YC01 and YC02 (originating from herpes zoster and varicella patients respectively) more than 100 times in cell culture. The resulting high-passage viruses were sequenced and compared to low-passage equivalents. Intriguingly, ORF62 was found to be highly mutated with the four SNPs, which are fixed or near-fixation in the vOka vaccine strain, also present in at least one of the high passaged viruses, along with the stop codon mutation in ORF0. Furthermore, high-passage viruses, in contrast to low-passage ones, were able to grow in non-human cells (guinea pig cells). This indicates that serial passaging, under unnatural conditions, is probably responsible for the emergence of mutations, as the cells try to adapt to the new growth environment. These mutations could in turn render the virus attenuated in the natural host and probably change the ability or the way the virus interacts with certain host pathways, which are normally essential for the virus life cycle.The vOka vaccine skin attenuationIt is now well established that the attenuation of vOka relies on reduced replication in skin22 and the next paragraphs will provide a picture of what is currently understood on the mechanisms underlying the vOka skin attenuation.The skinThe human skin is composed of three layers in ascending order from the innermost to the outermost: hypodermis (mainly composed of subcutaneous white adipose tissue, SWAT), dermis (mostly a connective tissue) and epidermis (epithelial tissue).47,48 Of these, both the dermis and the epidermis are permissive to VZV infection, however the epidermis is the main location of viral replication and the site of formation of blistering lesions, which harbor the infectious VZV virions necessary for virus transmission.The dermisThe dermis contains a component of adipose tissue, which is adjacent to the hypodermis, called dermal white adipose tissue (DWAT); however, its major component is connective tissue, which also houses nerve terminations, blood vessels, HFs and sebaceous and sweat glands.47,48 The major cell type populating the dermis is fibroblasts. Dermal fibroblasts secrete proteins, notably among them collagen, which form the extracellular matrix (ECM), an essential constituent which provides elasticity, as well as firmness to the dermis.47,49 Other cell types in the dermis are immune cells, for instance, dendritic cells and macrophages, which contribute to most of the immune responses in the skin.49The epidermisDermis and epidermis are separated by the basement membrane, a layer made up of ECM proteins, which include a number of collagen proteins, notably collagen IV and VII47 (Figure 2).
Figure 2.Schematic of human skin with focus on the epidermis. The epidermis of the skin is made up of keratinocytes organised in layers (basal, spinous, granular, upper-granular and cornified, in ascending order), based on the cellular and protein expression changes that they undergo during differentiation. The dashed lines underline some of the major genes/proteins, which are differentially expressed during differentiation.Keratinocytes represent the preeminent cell type in the epidermis, however other cell types are sporadically present, including Merkel cells, melanocytes and Langerhans cells.47In the epidermis, keratinocytes are distributed in layers based on their differentiation status. These organize as the basal, spinous, granular, upper-granular and cornified layers (in ascending order from the basement membrane). The basal layer is populated by a small number of epidermal stem cells and by undifferentiated keratinocytes, which still retain their ability to proliferate. As keratinocytes receive stimuli to differentiate, they cease to proliferate and to express certain genes (typically, but not exclusively, keratin 5 (K5) and keratin 14 (K14)), and start to express genes specific of the differentiated status (such as K1, K10, involucrin (IVL), loricrin, small proline-rich proteins (SPRRs), trichohyalin (TCHH) and filaggrin (FLG)50,51 (Figure 2). Terminal differentiation is also accompanied by a program of cell death called cornification, which starts at the level of the granular layer and leads to the loss of nuclei and organelles and the formation of the cornified envelope, a lining made of keratins and other proteins crosslinked together and embedded in a matrix of insoluble lipids.50,52 It is the insoluble and rigid nature of the cornified envelope that guarantees the physical barrier necessary for protection from external factors (such as pathogens or chemical factors), as well as to prevent water loss.A number of keratins are expressed in the skin of specific epithelia, for instance, keratins K2 and K9 are expressed in the differentiated keratinocytes of thickened or palmoplantar skin regions, respectively.51 Keratins are a crucial component of the epidermal barrier function, they assemble in filaments called keratin intermediate filaments (KIFs), which run from the nuclei to the cell–cell desmosomes and provide the foundation around which the cornified envelope is formed.50 Importantly, more and more evidence is emerging about keratins not having solely a structural role in the epidermis, but also being involved in other functions, such as working as signaling molecules.53 For instance, this has been demonstrated for K17, which is involved in the skin DNA damage response (DDR)54 and we have observed that the degradation of K10 by VZV has a signaling role in inducing activation of autophagy pathways.55VZV skin replicationVZV is transported to the skin by T lymphocytes expressing skin-homing markers after initial infection of the upper respiratory tract mucosa epithelium.2,3 In the skin, VZV appears to first infect HFs cells5,6 and, in the interfollicular epidermis, VZV infects undifferentiated basal keratinocytes.4 The predilection of VZV for infecting undifferentiated rather than differentiated keratinocytes has been confirmed in the calcium-switch model of VZV infection where it was also demonstrated that VZV copy number increases when keratinocytes move from an undifferentiated to a differentiated status.56 This is concomitant with an increase in the expression of early and late viral proteins with differentiation, indicating that VZV requires epidermal differentiation to fully mature into infectious cell-free virions that ultimately will be released by epidermal blisters.56 However, which cells VZV specifically targets in the HFs is still unclear. Furthermore, how the virus moves from the HFs to the interfollicular basal keratinocytes is yet to be determined.The skin epidermis is crucial to VZV life cycle; it is the major location of VZV replication, but also the site of virus transmission to new hosts, as well as the place where VZV gets access to the terminal endings of the sensory ganglia to establish latency. Despite its importance in the VZV life cycle, the mechanisms of VZV interaction with the skin host are still considerably unexplored. This is largely because VZV infectivity is restricted to humans and this limits the availability of suitable models of VZV infection. The Arvin group developed an in vivo model based on the infection of human skin tissues xenografted onto SCID-hu mice.2,22,57 Models developed in vitro include the calcium-switch model of VZV infection, which is based on infection of human primary or immortalized keratinocytes, which are then differentiated by addition of calcium to the cells culture23,55,56 and 3D in vitro models have been established based on infection of organotypic human skin cultures or human skin explants.55,56,58The known mechanisms of VZV infection and replication in the skin have been recently extensively reviewed.8,59 Here, we summarize only the hitherto established interactions of VZV with epidermal pathways, which include interaction with epidermal proteins, autophagy and apoptosis pathways, as well as epidermal innate immunity pathways (Figure 3a).
Figure 3.Schematic of the main host changes in keratinocytes infected with pOka and vOka. a) Following VZV infection, there is upregulation of a number of kallikreins, accompanied by downregulation of some of their targets, corneodesmosomal proteins DSG1 and DSC1. Keratins K1 and K10 are downregulated at the gene level. K10 downregulation is concomitantly caused by protein degradation, which is mediated by increased levels of MDM2. Decrease of K10 in turns determines upregulation of NR4A1, which induces autophagy. The autophagic flux is not completed and lysosomal proteins are downregulated. Other keratins are upregulated by VZV, notably K4, K13, K19 and K15. K17 appears to be upregulated at the protein level, although this was not observed at the gene level (#). In VZV-infected keratinocytes inhibitors of apoptosis pSTAT3 and survivin are upregulated, whereas the innate immunity mediators IFNα, pSTAT1 and PML-NB are downregulated. b) Keratin K15 is not upregulated by vOka in infected keratinocytes. The autophagic flux appears not to be as downregulated as by wild-type VZV in vOka infection of fibroblasts, but this remains to be confirmed in keratinocytes (*).RNAseq transcriptional analysis of primary keratinocytes in the calcium-switch model of VZV infection has highlighted a number of changes in the host epidermis characteristic of skin blistering diseases60; downregulation of the spinous keratins K1 and K10 and of cell–cell adhesive junctions, notably the corneodesmosomal proteins desmoglein-1 (DSG1) and desmocollin-1 (DSC1).56 This was associated with a generalized increase in the expression of serine proteases called kallikreins, of which two of the most upregulated, kallikrein 5 (KLK5) and KLK7, are proteases responsible for epidermal desquamation. The upregulation of KLK5 and KLK7 may account for a desquamation phenotype, which may facilitate the virus release from the epidermal cornified layer.56Notably, it has been demonstrated that keratin K10 downregulation in VZV infection is not only caused by a decrease in gene expression but also by proteosomal degradation following MDM2-mediated ubiquitination. MDM2 cytoplasmic expression is increased by KLK6, which is not normally associated with epidermal desquamation and yet was one of the most highly upregulated kallikreins in VZV infection of keratinocytes.55,56 Moreover, K10 plays a signaling role in VZV infection of keratinocytes; lack of K10 upregulates the transcription factor nuclear receptor subfamily 4 group A member 1 (NR4A1), which in turn induces activation of autophagy pathways.55 Autophagy has been reported both in keratinocytes and fibroblasts to be proviral for VZV and therefore suggested as a mechanism that VZV exploits for its life cycle.55,61,62 In keratinocytes, the autophagy flux appears to be incomplete; lysosomal proteins have a reduced expression, suggesting that the autophagic flux is not terminated with the fusion of autophagosomes/amphisomes with lysosomes.55Transcriptomic analysis of VZV-infected keratinocytes also revealed a number of other alterations in the host cells, such as increase in the expression of K15 and K19 and the mucosal keratins K4/13. K15 is expressed by stem cells of the HFs and, in the interfollicular epidermis, by basal keratinocytes,51,56,63 whereas K19 is expressed mainly by simple epithelia, but an association with stem cells has also been suggested.51,64 While the importance of K15 upregulation in VZV skin replication has been further demonstrated by knockdown or overexpression of K15, which led, respectively, to decreased or increased viral replication,23 the relevance of K4/13 and K19 upregulation in VZV infection has yet to be addressed. It may be that some of these keratins are upregulated as a compensatory response to K10 downregulation. Further investigation is also required to understand whether wound healing pathways may be involved in VZV skin replication, as it has been found that K17 (expression of which increments during wound healing65) and WNT5a proteins are upregulated in VZV-infected skin of SCID-hu mice.66 However, K17 was not increased at the mRNA level in the transcriptomic analysis of VZV-infected keratinocytes.56It has been demonstrated in investigations of VZV-infected skin tissues from SCID-hu mice that in the keratinocytes surrounding the epidermal blister, there is increase in the expression and activity of interferon-α (IFNα) along with other associated innate immunity regulators (e.g. phosphorylated signal transducer and activator of transcription 1, pSTAT1). Conversely, these are inhibited in correspondence of the lesion, suggesting that while VZV represses innate immunity pathways in the host cells, the uninfected surrounding keratinocytes mount an immune barrier, to keep the lesion contained (reviewed in3,59). Moreover, VZV inhibits the host promyelocytic leukemia-nuclear bodies (PML-NB), which confine the nascent virions in the cell nuclei to preclude them from completing their life cycle.67 VZV also interferes with the host cell apoptotic pathways, by increasing the levels of phosphorylated STAT3 (pSTAT3), and therefore of its downstream protein survivin, which is a cellular apoptosis inhibitor.68vOka skin replicationThe attenuation of vOka for replication in skin was demonstrated in vivo by Moffat et al.22 in SCID-hu mouse skin xenografts and in vitro in human primary keratinocytes,23 but not in other cell types, such as T lymphocytes,2 human neurons,24 lung fibroblasts or melanoma cells,22,69 confirming that the attenuation is likely to be keratinocyte-specific.What mechanisms are at the basis of vOka epidermal attenuation is still the subject of ongoing investigation. Immunity may play a role, as suggested by a study performed in dermal immune cells derived from human skin biopsies, where it was demonstrated that while VZV inhibits the signaling from pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) to Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) expressed by dendritic cells (DCs), vOka fails to do so, suggesting vOka may not evade immune responses as successfully as wild-type VZV.70 However, further studies will be required to understand how vOka interconnects with innate immunity in the epidermis.Because VZV interacts with specific epidermal immune and cellular pathways for its replication, understanding how the vOka strain interacts with these same pathways may uncover its attenuation mechanism. With this vision, some of the pathways and gene/protein expression changes described in the previous paragraph and summarized in Figure 3a, have been analyzed in the context of vOka skin infection (Figure 3b). Investigation into autophagy pathways in MRC-5 fibroblasts showed that the inhibition of the late stages of autophagic flux in vOka infection, is not as marked as in the wild-type VZV infection,71 however this remains to be confirmed in keratinocytes. Recently, it was shown in human primary keratinocytes in the calcium-switch model of VZV infection that K15 expression is not upregulated by vOka. Moreover, exogenous increase in K15 expression was sufficient to increase vOka replication and bring it to levels similar to pOka, suggesting that the failure of vOka to upregulate K15 may be one of the factors underpinning its attenuation.23 It may be speculated that both innate immune and cellular mechanisms may be involved in the attenuation; the vOka virus may not be as capable as the wild-type counterpart of inhibiting/evading the innate immune responses erected by the host and at the same time it may not be as capable of harnessing certain epidermal cellular pathways for replication. In both cases, very little is known, and further investigation is warranted.vOka mutations and skin attenuationSince, as described in paragraph “The genetics of the vOka vaccine virus”, distinct sequencing-based studies19–21,43,44,46 have concurred in the description of the same core mutations in ORF62 and the same stop codon mutation in ORF0, and being both these ORFs essential to VZV replication,3,72 ORF62 and ORF0 have been the primary focus in attempts to find cues for vOka attenuation. Nevertheless, non-sequencing-based studies have also identified two additional ORFs, ORF14 (gC) and ORF31 (gB), possible candidates.Below, we provide an overview of the current understanding of the putative involvement of ORF0, ORF14, ORF31 and ORF62 in vOka skin attenuation.ORF0 stop codon mutationORF0, also known as ORF S/L, was discovered later than the other VZV ORFs,73 and to date not much is known about its physiological function in VZV life cycle and pathogenesis. ORF0 contains a signal for VZV DNA packaging72 and is considered to be essential for VZV replication, as its deletion caused reduced viral growth in infected MeWo cells and the skin of SCID-hu mice.74The mutation at position 560 of ORF0 removes a stop codon and the extended C-terminus of the ORF0 protein is present in the virion surface where it gets N-glycosylated, a feature that is not shared with pOka-ORF0.75 However, in studies performed in MeWo cells, replacing ORF0 in the pOka strain with the vOka variant did not lead to an attenuated phenotype nor did the deletion of the extended glycosylated C-terminus of vOka-ORF0.75 This may suggest that other mutations may have a synergistic effect and warrants further investigations. Furthermore, a study focusing on the VZV Ellen strain, which bears the same ORF0 stop codon mutation, has suggested that this mutation may have a role in attenuation, but this has not been evaluated in skin.43ORF14 reduced expressionORF14 encodes the VZV glycoprotein gC (initially named gpV), which was first described in 1990, and whose function is still under investigation. Since its discovery, it has been observed that the vaccine strain vOka accumulates low levels of gC compared with its parental strain, raising questions regarding the possible involvement of gC in the skin attenuation of vOka.76 In support of this hypothesis Moffat et al. 22 showed that the absence of gC expression is associated with diminished replication of VZV in the skin of SCID-hu mice. The same study demonstrated that although not required for viral growth in vitro, gC might be critical for VZV virulence in vivo. Nevertheless, a direct correlation between reduced expression of gC and the attenuation of vOka in skin has not yet been demonstrated.In mutational analysis studies of the vOka vaccine strain (and commercial vaccine derivates), ORF14 was not found to include any significant SNPs; of the four reported, the only SNP leading to NS mutation (aa position 499) has low allele frequency (2.08%), two SNPs lead to synonymous mutations (aa 490 and 360 with allele frequency of 1.02% and 1.69%, respectively) and one leads to a change from ocher stop codon (TAA) to amber stop codon (TAG) (aa 561 with 14.58% allele frequency).19–21 Of note, the latter is shared by the majority of the live attenuated vaccines (Suduvax, Varilrix, Varivax20,21,77 and Baike).44 However, this being a stop codon mutation, it appears unlikely that this may play a role in attenuation. This raises the question as to what determines low gC expression in vOka. It was hypothesized that this could be caused by the promoter of ORF14 being under the influence of the major transactivator IE62, which is well recognized to be highly mutated in the vaccine variant. This theory was, however, disproven, as the ORF14 promoter was found not to be regulated by IE62.19 Another possible explanation is based on the observation that gC is expressed late in the VZV life cycle (at about 72 h post-infection, whereas other glycoproteins such as gE and gB are already synthesized within 4–6 h after infection). Therefore, multiple passaging of the virus (process used for the creation of the vaccine) may lead to the diminished expression of gC, as the virus does not have enough time to start gC synthesis. Additionally, gC expression was found to be enhanced by treatment with hexamethylene bisacetamide (HMBA) and retinoic acid, by acting on the PBX/HOX transcription factors. All in all, these observations indicate that the gC content of a given VZV strain could heavily depend on the cell culture conditions and the production methods of the vaccine.78,79The G-quadruplex (G4) structure is a type of secondary structure that DNA and RNA nucleic acids can form in guanine-rich sequences. Four guanine bases interact with each other forming a square plane (or tetrad). Up to four guanine tetrads can associate further, forming stacks. The G4 structures are hypothesized to be involved in a number of cellular processes spanning from regulation of transcription and translation to epigenetic regulation.80 In the VZV genome (Dumas or pOka sequences references used), ORF14 is predicted to be enriched with stable G4 structures, which suppress the expression of gC. Mutations that disrupt some of the G4 structures led to increased expression of gC, while they reduced viral growth and cell-to-cell spread in MeWo cells and human foreskin fibroblasts.81 The observation that increased expression of gC leads to an attenuated phenotype disagrees with the hypothesis that decreased gC expression could be one of the factors responsible for the attenuation of the vaccine strain and therefore necessitates further investigations. Notably, the area of the VZV genome where G4 structures have been predicted to form (nt 20,601–20,925 of the pOka sequence) is outside the region containing SNPs in ORF14 in the vOka genome. Overall, the findings on the putative role of gC in vOka attenuation are not clear and require further study.ORF31 mutationORF31 encodes the VZV glycoprotein gB, which forms a trimer by associating with the gH-gL heterodimer. Together they form the membrane fusion complex necessary for viral entry into the cells by mediating the fusion of the viral envelope with the target cell’s membrane. The fusion complex also mediates cell-to-cell fusion, which leads to syncytia formation, a characteristic phenotype of VZV cells infection (reviewed in82).A recent study has highlighted the implication in vOka attenuation of the SNP located at nucleotide position 2096 of the ORF31 coding sequence. In pOka, at nucleotide 2096, almost half of the genome sequences harbor a guanine base (G), while the other half an alanine base (A); G leads to the translation of an arginine at amino acid position 699 (699 R), whereas A results in a glutamine (699Q). Interestingly, this equilibrium between G and A is disturbed in the vOka genome, where most of the bases (>99.98) at this position are represented by A, hence gB carries almost exclusively a glutamine at position 669. A pOka strain engineered to express only the 699Q variant displayed a vOka-like phenotype; the 699Q variant was less efficient in allowing viral entry into neurons and replicated less in skin fibroblasts.83 Additionally, it was shown that in cell-free viruses expressing both SNP variants in equal amount, after entry into neuronal cells, the 669 R variant was favored over 699Q.83 These results strongly suggest that the change in the dominant amino acid at position 669 of vOka gB could contribute to the vOka attenuation in skin. Interestingly, this seems to affect fibroblasts and not keratinocytes.83 More work will be required to understand how this aminoacidic change could mechanistically disfavor the vOka growth and whether this would represent a mechanism of attenuation in the dermis, rather than the epidermis.ORF62 mutationsORF62 encodes the immediate early protein IE62, which is essential for viral replication in skin. IE62 is the major transactivator of VZV; it induces gene transcription of immediate early, early, and late viral genes, by interacting with the host transcription factor SP1.3,84 As described in Paragraph “The genetics of the vOka vaccine virus”, ORF62 is the most highly mutated ORF in the vOka vaccine and its commercial derivatives, but also in other attenuated vaccines developed from different parental strains, as well as in vaccine-associated rashes.19–21,38,44,46,77 Moreover, some of the mutations in the ORF62 gene were found to be reverted to wild-type allele in the virus recovered from vaccine rashes, compared to the vOka inoculum, further suggesting that mutations in this protein may be critical for vaccine attenuation.85The fact that distinct studies have all converged on reporting the same core of mutations in ORF62 and the fact that these include five out of the six fixed or near-fixed mutations in all the vOka preparations (Figure 1 and Table 1) identifies the mutated ORF62 as a likely player in vOka attenuation. A number of investigations have researched whether and how the vOka ORF62 mutations may affect vOka replication in skin and therefore account for its attenuated phenotype. Because of IE62 role as transactivator, many studies have initially focused on whether vOka IE62 transcriptional activity is impaired.Gomi et al. 2002 employed a luciferase assay and ectopically expressed IE62, either wild-type or mutated. The mutated IE62 included the eight NS substitutions that were identified by the same study at the time. The assay showed that the mutated variant exhibited less transactivation activity.19 Another study showed that vOka infection of MRC-5 fibroblasts leads to decreased transcription of ORFs 62, 65, 66 and 67. It was suggested that IE62 mutations may lead to decreased expression of proteins important for viral spread and thereby cause attenuation.86 Nevertheless, luciferase-based assays from the same study, using either pOka or vOka IE62 did not demonstrate a statistically significant difference in the expression of those ORFs.In a study investigating the Suduvax vaccine, it was found that, in infected MeWo cells, Suduvax IE62 could transactivate ORFs 4, 28, 29, and 68 less efficiently compared to its wild-type equivalent. However, no significant effect on its activity was observed upon introducing the individual mutations.87 Interestingly, although the Suduvax vaccine is not based on the vOka strain, it shares with it six NS mutations, of which two 107,252 (S628G) and 106,262 (R958G), are the two most fixed NS mutations present in vOka ORF62 (Figure 1). This evidence reinforces the hypothesis that reduced transactivation activity of IE62 caused by the acquired mutations could represent one of the drivers of viral attenuation.As described in paragraph “vOka skin replication” and Figure 3b, we have observed in work performed in human primary keratinocytes, that vOka (VariVax strain) does not increase the expression of the keratin K15, which is on the other end essential for successful VZV replication in the epidermis.23 IE62 appears to be the VZV protein responsible for the upregulation of K15 during VZV infection, therefore we investigated whether its vOka-mutated version may fail in this role. The vOka version of ORF62 containing all the five near-fixed mutations (and four additional ones present at various levels in the different vOka-based vaccine preparations), was not able to upregulate K15 expression. This was accompanied by inability of vOka IE62 to rescue viral replication in cells that were infected with the vOka virus, compared to cells infected with vOka and expressing the pOka version of IE62.23 This evidence suggests that the vOka-mutated IE62 may have lost its ability to interact with certain host epidermal pathways, for example, K15 (and downstream pathways) and this may contribute to the virus not being able to replicate as well in skin. Because the observations regarding IE62 reported in this paragraph are based on transfection studies of the mutated IE62 protein, further investigations using infection with the VZV virus carrying single mutations in IE62 may prove valuable to better elucidate the role of mutated IE62 in vOka attenuation.In a recent publication, the 3D structure of IE62 was analyzed using the artificial intelligence algorithm AlphaFold2. The currently licensed live attenuated vaccines against varicella based on three different parental strains, pOka (VariVax, VarilRix), Oka/SK (SKY Varicella), and MAV/06 (Suduvax) were studied, and the IE62 structure from each was predicted and compared to the pOka strain. The IE62 protein from SKY Varicella was predicted to have the same structure as IE62 from the non-attenuated pOka strain, whereas the structure analysis of IE62 proteins from VariVax, VarilRix or Suduvax displayed a conformational change of an alpha-helix located in the region 1 of the protein. It could be hypothesized that such conformational change might hinder the IE62 interactome and lead to diminished virulence.39 Nevertheless, further research is required to better understand how such a conformational change would affect the interaction of VZV with certain host pathways and lead to attenuation, as well as to test this in skin models.Conclusions and future perspectivesSeveral studies on the genetics of vOka have exposed the highly mutated nature of the vOka virus compared to the parental VZV and highlighted that fixed or near-fixed mutations in all the vOka vaccine preparations lie in ORF62 and ORF0, both essential genes in VZV replication. However, much of the focus to date has been on the molecular biology of the virus, rather than on the cell biology of the host with which it needs to interconnect to replicate. Understanding how host epidermal pathways are altered upon vOka infection and how this differs from its wild-type counterpart, will shed light on the mechanisms of vOka attenuation.Of the most highly mutated genes in vOka, ORF62, being the only mutated gene with a regulatory function in the VZV life cycle and being the gene containing five out of the six near-fixed mutations among all the vOka strains, has been the most closely interrogated. In a keratinocyte model of VZV infection, correlation between mutations in ORF62 and reduced vOka viral growth has been demonstrated, along with a defective interaction with the epidermal protein keratin K15, which is normally increased by VZV to facilitate replication in the epidermis.23 However, it is plausible that more than one mechanism accounts for the vOka attenuated phenotype, as also demonstrated by an investigation that used recombinant chimeric viruses containing different areas of the pOka or vOka genomes but was not able to attribute attenuation to a single area of the genome.69 Therefore, further studies on other genes that are highly mutated in vOka, such as ORF0 and ORF31, or genes that have differential expression such as ORF14, are warranted.Modern technologies, such as single cell sequencing and spatial omics techniques, associated with the use of models of human skin cultures that closely mimic epidermal differentiation (e.g. skin organotypics/organoids, skin explants or the calcium-switch keratinocytes models) may allow better understanding of how vOka interacts with specific epidermal pathways (innate immunity, keratinocyte differentiation, autophagy), in distinct epidermal layers and at specific times of the vOka life cycle. This, combined with the generation of vOka derivatives bearing single mutations (e.g. each of the single NS mutations in ORF62) may pinpoint the mutation/mutations responsible for the attenuation and their functional impact.Understanding how the vOka vaccine is attenuated for skin replication will pave the way for the development of new non-live vaccines, which will minimize possible, although rare, vaccine-associated adverse effects. This will also, by comparative studies, provide a better understanding of the wild-type VZV skin pathogenesis.


Title: Nosocomial transmission of chickenpox and varicella zoster virus seroprevalence rate amongst healthcare workers in a teaching hospital in China

BackgroundVaricella zoster virus (VZV) causes two clinically distinct forms of disease: varicella (chickenpox), as a primary infection, and zoster (shingles) due to reactivation of latent VZV [1–3]. The transmission of VZV occurs via inhalation of airborne droplets or direct contact with vesicular fluid from skin lesions. VZV infection is considered an occupational hazard for susceptible healthcare workers (HCWs), as it can spread to other susceptible coworkers and patients [4]. Transmission of VZV among HCWs and patients has been reported [5–7]. Current policy in China for prevention of nosocomial transmission of VZV is prompt recognition of patients with suspected VZV infection with airborne isolation in negative pressure single room if possible, however mandatory VZV IgG testing is still not yet implemented. Thus HCWs with negative history of chickenpox and VZV vaccination should be screened for VZV antibodies. Immune status to VZV can be assessed by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISAs), or fluorescent antibody to membrane antigen (FAMA) assays [8]. Seronegative HCWs are considered susceptible to varicella, therefore VZV vaccination is recommended [4].Primary VZV infection is usually self-limiting in immunocompetent hosts, however, the severity increases with age. Furthermore, as HCWs care for patients in different wards and units, there is a high potential of nosocomial transmission among HCWs and patients if the HCW is infected, especially when the infectious period of VZV starts 2 days before the onset of rash. The situation would be worse if the infected HCW is involved in taking care of pregnant women and immunocompromised individuals (such as patients receiving high dose immunosuppressant or history of transplantation), as primary VZV infection in immunocompromised patients can be fulminant, and it can present as encephalitis, pneumonitis and hepatitis. The mortality rate of primary VZV infection could be up to 7% if left untreated. As a result, nosocomial transmission of VZV should never be overlooked.As nosocomial transmission of varicella is seldom reported in China, this study aims to report three nosocomial transmissions of chickenpox, and investigate the seroprevalence rate of VZV among healthcare workers in a tertiary teaching hospital in China.MethodsOutbreak investigation and management of nosocomial transmission of chickenpoxRetrospective case finding for nosocomial transmission of chickenpox was conducted, with specific attention being paid to infection control measures and outbreak investigations between January 1, 2013 and December 31, 2017. The clinical definition of varicella is “an illness with acute onset of diffuse (generalized) papulovesicular rash without other apparent cause”. All contacts in the hospital were followed up by the infection control unit staff to determine the number of susceptible contacts (non-immune to varicella) by contact tracing. Susceptible contacts were put under self-medical surveillance and requested to refrain from patient contact from Day 8 after 1st exposure to Day 21 after last exposure. Individuals were considered susceptible if they did not fulfill any one of the following criteria: 1) History of varicella; 2) Completion of varicella vaccine according to recommended schedule; 3) Positive serum VZV IgG. Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for susceptible contacts were administered according to CDC recommendations [2].Seroprevalence study of HCWs VZV antibodiesA cross-sectional study on the seroprevalence rate of VZV among healthcare workers (HCWs) was conducted between January 1, 2014 and December 31, 2017 in a tertiary teaching hospital in China, with 1804 hospital staff including doctors, nurses, technicians and non-clinical workers participated in this study. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the hospital. Through questionnaire, information including demographic data, history of varicella and vaccination were collected from the participants. Blood samples were collected from each individual and the serum VZV antibodies were measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) using commercial kit (Beier, Beijing, China; based on manufacturer’s data, the positive cutoff was defined as 0.15 if mean of absorbance of negative control < 0.05, while 0.1 + mean of absorbance of negative control if mean of absorbance of negative control ≥0.05, with sensitivity and specificity quoted as 96.1 and 100% respectively).Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS 20 software. Categorical variables were compared using Chi-square test. A P-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Positive predictive value (PPV) and negative predictive value (NPV) of a self-reported history of varicella were calculated, with a positive serum VZV IgG considered as the gold standard of immunity against VZV.Economic evaluation of nosocomial transmissionIn order to assess the economic impact of nosocomial transmission of VZV, two important parameters, person-days of work lost and infection control unit person-hours, were assessed. Person-days of work lost is defined as the total number of days of work loss in clinical staff for both susceptible contacts and infected cases. Infection control unit person-hours is defined as the number of hours required for infection control unit for outbreak investigation and control. The cost of performing VZV IgG ELISA was also calculated based on the price of equipment together with the manpower required to perform the test.ResultsOutbreak investigation and controlThere were three episodes of nosocomial transmission of varicella involving 8 individuals, in which 4 HCWs (including one doctor, one non-clinical worker and two nursing students) were infected nosocomially. Table 1 shows the characteristics of the 8 cases of varicella, and Fig. 1 shows the epidemic curve and chain of transmission in these episodes.Table 1Characteristics of 8 chickenpox cases in three nosocomial transmissions, 2013–2017EventCase no.OccupationUnderlying disease or PregnancyDate of rash onsetSymptomsTransmission settingTotal contactsfevergeneralized vesicular rashsore throatNosocomial transmission 1231NA (Patient)No15/04/2013++–Community2Doctor (HCW)No05/05/2013+++HospitalNosocomial transmission 2173Non-clinical staff(HCW)No10/08/2013–+–Community4Non-clinical staff(HCW)No22/08/2013+++HospitalNosocomial transmission 3875Nursing student(HCW)No20/03/2017++–Community6Nursing student(HCW)No20/03/2017++–Community7Nursing student(HCW)No05/04/2017++–Hospital8Nursing student(HCW)No07/04/2017++–HospitalFig. 1Timeline illustrating epidemic curve and chain of nosocomial transmission of chickenpox in our study, 2013–2017Nosocomial transmission 1On May 5, 2013, a paediatrician (Case 2) presented with fever followed by generalized vesicular rash. She recalled contacting a patient (Case 1) with chickenpox on April 18, 2013 in the hospital, and she was susceptible to VZV, i.e., she was neither vaccinated nor previously infected with VZV. She was diagnosed to have varicella and requested self-isolation to prevent ongoing transmission. Contact tracing was initiated by the hospital infection control unit and a total of 23 healthcare worker contacts were identified with advice on prodromal symptoms to ensure they were not exposed to other susceptible HCWs or patients. No further new cases were identified after the above infection control measures. After this incident, serum VZV IgG testing for HCW was introduced by hospital health direction.Nosocomial transmission 2On August 22, 2013, a non-immune operator from the hospital reception center (Case 4) presented with fever, generalized vesicular rash and sore throat. She recalled one of her colleagues (Case 3), who worked with her in the same office, developed chickenpox during August 10–17, 2013. She was subsequently diagnosed to have varicella. The infection control unit was informed of the incident, with 17 healthcare worker contacts identified through contact tracing. Further history taking and laboratory testing suggested 4 of the 17 contacts were susceptible, therefore they all received post-exposure prophylaxis with oral acyclovir. No further new cases were identified after the above infection control measures.Nosocomial transmission 3On March 20, 2017, two nursing students (Case 5 and Case 6) from hospital outsourcing company reported to have fever and generalized vesicular rash. They worked as nursing assistants in the hospital and lived in a 8-person dormitory room. They were diagnosed to have varicella and requested self-isolation. The infection control unit was informed, with 42 healthcare worker contacts identified through contact tracing. Thorough investigation suggested 5 out of 42 contacts were susceptible. All susceptible contacts received VZV vaccination as Post-exposure Prophylaxis (PEP), with recommendation on self-isolation during incubation period provided.On April 5, 2017 and April 7, 2017, two nursing students (Case 7 and Case 8), who lived with Case 5 in the same dormitory, presented with similar clinical manifestations as Case 5, with VZV DNA detected from the vesicular fluid of skin lesions in both nursing students by PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction). These two infected individuals were not classified as susceptible contacts during the first round of contact tracing, because both of them volunteered previous history of VZV vaccination. A further 45 healthcare worker contacts were identified through second round of contact tracing, and 4 out of 45 contacts were classified as susceptible individuals, with subsequent post-exposure prophylaxis provided. No further new cases were identified after the above infection control measures.Seroprevalence of VZV in HCWsOf the 1804 HCWs participated, there were 215 (11.9%) male and 1589 (88.1%) female HCWs, with their ages ranging from 17 to 60 years (median age: 27 years). Table 2 shows the demographic characteristics of the participated HCWs. The overall seroprevalence rate of VZV was 88.4%. The seroprevalence rates of HCWs with different genders and occupations showed no statistically significant differences. HCWs aged ≥36 years were found to have the highest seroprevalence rate (92.6%), while HCWs aged ≤25 years were found to have the lowest seroprevalence rate (85.2%).Table 2Demographic data and VZV serostatus of 1804 healthcare workersVariableTotal no.
