Heart punction was performed to collect blood. Serum was isolated following clotting of the blood at +4°C, centrifugation and supernatant was collected and stored at −20°C. Swabs of the skin of the lumbosacral region (i.c.), of the tail (i.c. and i.n.), and of the legs (i.n.) were collected in 500 µl PBS containing 2% FCS (PBS 2%) and stored at −20°C. Lymph nodes, spleen, liver, lungs, back skin, tail and leg were dissected aseptically. Lymph nodes and spleen were processed separately, and the isolated cells were used for flow cytometry and viral DNA quantification. Liver, lungs and back skin were collected in PBS 2%, weighed, frozen at −20°C, and homogenized prior DNA extraction. All DNA extractions were performed by using QIAamp® DNA Mini and blood Mini kits (Qiagen, Venlo, Netherlands) following manufacturer's instructions, and samples were then subjected to quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR).SeroneutralizationPlaque neutralization assays were performed in 96-well microplates. Each serum was tested individually. Sera were diluted 1 10 in MEM 2%, inactivated for 30 min at 56°C and two-fold dilutions were done to reach 1 640. CML1, diluted in MEM 2% to a concentration of 100 TCID50 in 100 µl, was added to each well containing the sera to test and to the virus-control wells. The microplates were incubated for 2 h at 37°C. HEL cells, resuspended in MEM 2%, were then added at a concentration of 2.8×104 cells per 80 µl per well. Microplates were incubated for 3 days at 37°C and examined for plaque formation. The neutralization titer was calculated using the Spearman-Karber formula which is the negative logarithm of the highest dilution of serum that caused a 50% reduction in the number of wells exhibiting CPE. The assays included virus control, cell control, negative controls of uninfected animals and controls to evaluate potential toxicity of the serum alone.Viral DNA detectionqPCR targeting the CMP48L gene (homolog of the F13L gene of VACV strain Copenhagen) was used to quantify viral DNA. qPCR was done on 5 µl of total DNA extracted in a 20 µl reaction volume using the TaqMan® Fast Universal PCR master mix, forward primer [5′-CAA CTC CAT TAT AGA AGC CAT T-3′], reverse primer [5′-CGT VGT TCT TAT CCC AAT TAC CA-3′], and an MGB probe [6-FAM-ATA GAG GAG TTA AGA TCA GAC TT-MGB] (Applied Biosystems, Halle, Belgium and Warrington, UK). Reactions were processed by using the SDS7500Fast apparatus. Plasmid DNA containing the CMP48L gene was used to obtain the standard curve and to determine the DNA copy numbers per sample. The limit of detection per 5 µl sample was 10 DNA copies.HistopathologyOne mouse of each group, i.e., group uninfected or group CML1, was euthanized and various tissue samples, such as skin, tail, leg, lungs, lymph nodes, were collected for histological examinations. Samples were fixed for one day in formol 6% and then placed in PBS. Samples were embedded in paraffin and 5 micrometer sections were stained with hematoxylin-eosin.Preparation of cell suspensionsSpleen and pool of draining lymph nodes (DLNs; inguinal, axillary, mesenteric and lumbar lymph nodes) were isolated from 4 individual mice in each group and processed separately. Organs were disrupted in cold PBS 2%, and filtered through a 70 µm nylon cell strainer. For all procedures, cell suspensions were kept on ice and washings were done with cold PBS 2%. Cell suspensions from the spleen were washed once, treated with ammonium chloride and washed again. Lymph node cells were only washed once. Cells were then counted before antibody (Ab) staining.Flow cytometryThe following conjugated Abs, purchased from eBioscience (San Diego, CA, USA), were used: anti-CD19-FITC (clone 1D3), anti-Ly-6G (Gr1)-FITC (clone RB6-8C5), anti-CD11c-FITC (clone N418), anti-CD45R (B220)-PE (clone RA3-6B2), anti-F4/80-PE (clone BM8), anti-CD11b-APC (clone M1/70), anti-pan-NK cells (CD49b)-APC (clone DX5). Cell suspensions obtained from the spleen and lymph nodes (106 cells/tube) were blocked with a 1/3 dilution of FcR Blocking Reagent (Miltenyi Biotec, Bergisch Gladbach, Germany) for 20 min at 4°C, and then stained in PBS 2% for 20 min at 4°C with the Ab of interest. Cells were washed once with cold PBS 2% between each Ab staining, and washed twice before fixation with a 3% formaldehyde solution. Fluorescence was acquired on a total of 2×104 cells (spleen) or 1.5×104 cells (lymph nodes) with a FACSCalibur flow cytometer (BD Biosciences, San Jose, CA, USA) and the data were analyzed with the Cellquest software (BD Biosciences).Cytokine assaysThe sera of each group of mice were used for cytokine detection. IL-1β, IL-2, IL-4, IL-5, IL-6, IL-10, IL-13, IL-17, IL-18, GM-CSF, IFN-γ, TNF-α, M-CSF were measured using the kit Bio-Plex Pro™ Mouse cytokine multiplex Assay (Biorad, Nazareth Eke, Belgium), according to manufacturer's instructions. IL-6 immunoassays were performed using the kit Quantitine® (R&D Systems, Minneapolis, US), according to manufacturer's instructions. Only cytokine levels over 10 pg/ml were considered for statistical analyses.Statistical analysesAll statistical analyses were done with GraphPad Prism 5 software (GraphPad Software Inc., La Jolla, CA, USA). Viral loads and FACS results were analyzed with Mann Whitney test and unpaired Student t test, respectively, and survival curves with Log-rank (Mantel-Cox) test. Statistic significance was defined as follow: p<0.001 or ***, extremely significant; p<0.01 or **, very significant; p<0.05 or *, significant; and p>0.05 or ns, not significant.


Title: Prevention and Treatment of Monkeypox: A Step-by-Step Guide for Healthcare Professionals and General Population

Introduction and backgroundMonkeypox belongs to the same genus that causes smallpox. Many common viruses belong to this genus, including cowpox, horsepox, camelpox, and alaskapox. The variola virus is the most common and well-known member among all the viruses present in this genus. The World Health Organization (WHO) formally declared the eradication of smallpox in 1980 [1].Even though the monkeypox virus is homologous to the smallpox virus, the mortality risk and contact transmission from monkeypox are substantially lower than that of smallpox [2,3]. However, the signs and symptoms, primarily the rash, are very similar to smallpox. In Africa, two distinct lineages of the monkeypox virus are identified, clade 1 and clade 2. Clade 1 is predominantly prevalent in Central Africa and the Congo Basin, whereas clade 2 is restricted to West Africa [2]. The clade 2 strain of monkeypox is linked to the current monkeypox pandemic, triggering a global public health emergency. However, a recent study shows that the circulating strain of the virus has had multiple mutations in its DNA genome, which raises the possibility that the circulating virus is changing for human adaptation, and contagion [3].ReviewMethodologyA iterature search for monkeypox was performed using PubMed, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar search engines. The search syntax included the following terms: "Monkeypox" and "origin," "spread", "symptoms", "prevention", "treatment", "vaccine", OR "risk to the healthcare worker". Four physician authors reviewed the literature, and the information is summarized in this article for simplicity of comprehension.EpidemiologyMonkeypox was initially isolated in Denmark from monkeys used in the resource of poliovirus in 1959 [4]. Some sporadic monkey virus outbreaks have been seen in different animals since then. In the 1970s, researchers in Congo identified the first human case of monkeypox. Later, in the late 1970s, many instances of this virus were identified in Central and West Africa. Since the first monkeypox virus outbreak in the United States in 2003 [5], several sporadic cases have been observed in numerous non-endemic continents, including Europe and Asia. The current epidemic is widespread worldwide and exhibits person-to-person transmission (explained below). Figure 1 and Figure 2 show the total number of monkeypox cases worldwide as of August 12, 2022. The Center for Disease Control (CDC) publicly made the data available [6]. These figures highlight the countries most affected by the Monkeypox virus.Figure 1Monkeypox cases worldwideMonkeypox cases in the world as of August 12, 2022 [6]Figure 2Number of confirmed monkeypox cases by countryNumber of confirmed cases by country [6]Immunization against smallpox also protects humans against the monkeypox virus; after the smallpox vaccination program was abandoned due to the disease's eradication, the WHO was concerned about greater susceptibility and incidence of monkeypox infection in the contemporary population. A survey conducted between 2005-2007 in the Democratic Republic of Congo showed that monkeypox infection in this country rose by 20-fold [7].Early May 2022 saw the isolation of the first cases of the current major monkeypox outbreak in Europe [8], and since then, cases have risen globally, including in non-endemic nations. WHO declared monkeypox a public health emergency of international concern on July 23, 2022 [9], and it is soon to reach pandemic levels. Figure 3 and Figure 4 show the total number of monkeypox cases in the United States and their breakdown by state. Figure 5 shows the rising trend of monkeypox cases in the United States [6]. Figure 3States affected by monkeypoxStates affected by Monkeypox virus in the United States [6]Figure 4Breakdown of the total number of confirmed cases in the US by statesNumber of confirmed cases in the US by states [6]Figure 5Trends in the current outbreak of monkeypox cases in the United StatesTrends in the current outbreak of monkeypox cases in the United States since May 17, 2022 [6]The transmission of the monkeypox virus can happen in two waysAnimal to Human TransmissionDuring this transmission, humans come in contact with the virus via infected animals' body fluids or by an infected animal's bite. It can also be transmitted when consuming raw/minimally processed meat from an infected animal. This raw or minimally processed meat consumption is also known as bushmeat. The monkeypox virus in Africa is typically found in animals like squirrels, rats, and monkeys [10].Human to Human TransmissionHuman transmission can occur in different ways, which include direct contact, indirect contact, respiratory droplets, and vertical transmission [11-15].Direct contact: Transmission occurs when a person comes in direct contact with the infection source, for example, infected body fluids or scabs. The ongoing outbreak of monkeypox in the world, especially in non-endemic countries, is thought to be due to the person's direct contact, mostly during sexual activities [11]. A non-infected person gets exposed to the infectious material from the skin of an infected person with close physical contact and therefore acquires this infection [11,12].Indirect contact: Transmission occurs when materials like clothes or linens come in contact with infected material like bodily fluids. A non-infected person can then come in contact with these materials and get infected [13].Respiratory transmission: Transmission occurs via respiratory secretions/droplets from coughing and sneezing [14].Vertical transmission: Transmission occurs upon a fetus being exposed to the virus from her mother. The virus is known to cross the placenta and can lead to congenital monkeypox infection in newborn babies [15].Future studies are required to better comprehend the role of virus transmission through genital fluids versus other secretions/forms [16]. Hence, labeling the disease as a sexually transmitted disease will lead to the underutilization of preventive efforts, which will move us closer to a pandemic scenario [16].PathogenesisMonkeypox virus can be transmitted via animal or human contact, as described above. The virus enters the host, replicates at the entry site, and circulates via the lymphatic system. This leads to systemic infection, also known as primary viremia. The virus will now start replicating in the lymphoid organs and distant lymph nodes, resulting in infection of the epithelium and tertiary organs, producing mucosal and skin lesions, which results in the clinical manifestation of this virus [17].Clinical manifestationsThe incubation period for the monkeypox virus can range from five days to three weeks [17]. Monkeypox causes high-grade fever, chills, fatigue, lymphadenopathy, muscle pain, and vesicular eruptions with a rash. The prodromal phase is associated with all the symptoms but without a rash. The prodromal period lasts about four to five days. The rash typically appears after four to five days of fever and continues for two to three weeks (Figure 6, 7). Figure 6Monkeypox rash with pustulesReprinted from Ajmera et al. [18]Figure 7Monkeypox rashReprinted from Ajmera et al. [18]However, some patients can get the rash without going through the prodromal phase [14]. The rash typically appears on the face but can also be found on the palms of hands and soles of the feet. Recent cases of monkeypox infection are associated with the involvement of the genitalia, anus, and oral mucous membranes [19,20]. The rash looks like a macule of around 2 to 5 mm in diameter. These macules/lesions will subsequently develop into vesicles and pustules. The lesions are very well-circumscribed, with central umbilication/depression on top of the lesion. These lesions will eventually crust over, dry, and fall off the skin in about one to two weeks. The rash during the developmental phase can be painful but mostly becomes itchy during the healing phase, i.e., during the formation of the dry crust [21]. The lab findings associated with monkeypox infection are nonspecific and include abnormal liver function enzymes, leukocytosis, and even thrombocytopenia [22]. The mortality risk associated with monkeypox varies depending upon which strain a person is infected with, i.e., clade 1 vs. clade 2. The current outbreak of monkeypox is similar to clad 2 strain which is less virulent than clad 1. So far, till July 2022, close to 14,000 cases of monkeypox worldwide have been reported, which include five deaths in African nations [23]. Immunocompromised status, complicated infections causing end-organ damage, children younger than eight years old, pregnant or breastfeeding women, and monkeypox infection in unusual places, including the eyes, are independent predictors of disease severity [24].DiagnosisPatients with typical rash and symptoms such as fever/chills should be suspected of having monkeypox infection, particularly if they have risk factors like recent travel to areas endemic for monkeypox. Additionally, patients who experience symptoms of sexually transmitted infections, such as genital rash, and who do not improve after receiving empiric treatment should be treated with a high degree of suspicion.Laboratory evidence such as that of the predominance of the virus or IgM (immunoglobulin) antibodies must be present if monkeypox is suspected in the patient. Viral or serological testing can be used to determine this.Viral testing includes a polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test performed on the infected lesion. A patient whose PCR test result shows positive Orthopoxvirus is suspected of having monkeypox infection per CDC guidelines for the 2022 outbreak of the monkey virus. Confirmation of the virus can be made when monkey virus DNA can be demonstrated by PCR.Serological testing for the detection of monkeypox can be used if viral testing such as PCR is unavailable. The patient infected with the monkeypox virus will have elevated anti-Orthopoxvirus IgM & IgG antibodies, typically developing five to eight days after the rash [25].Monkeypox virus-infected cells have a brick-like form on electron microscopy identical to variola or vaccinia virus-infected cells, as seen in Figure 3.Figure 8Monkeypox virus infected cellsImage of monkeypox virus as seen from an electron microscopic in a human skin sample: CDC public health image library [26]TreatmentThe majority of monkeypox virus patients have mild symptoms and should make a full recovery without any professional attention. However, some patients could need hospitalization and supportive care due to nausea, vomiting, the potential for dehydration, or pain management. Antiviral medication is advised for those people who, as was previously noted, are at high risk of contracting a severe illness.Multiple antiviral medications are available which can be used for the treatment of monkeypox. Some of these medications were developed for treating smallpox in animals but are expected to have the same activity against monkeypox [24,25]. Of all the antivirals available, tecovirimat is a treatment of choice for most cases. Patients with severe disease may also benefit from dual therapy of tecovirimat and cidofovir. Public health officials should be made aware when starting these treatments.TecovirimatTecovirimat is available in both an IV and oral form. This medication inhibits the VP37 protein present in Orthopoxvirus and therefore blocks the interaction of the virus with the host cell. This leads to inhibition of the infectious virus particles and prevents the host cell from getting infected. In 2018, the United States (US) approved tecovirimat to treat the smallpox virus [27]. Tecovirimat's dose depends upon the patient's weight and renal functions (on the IV); the treatment duration is 14 days. The only contraindication of tecovirimat, when given in IV form, is a severe renal impairment with creatinine clearance <30 mL/min. The oral form, however, has no contraindication with any form of renal function. Tecovirimat has not been studied in pregnant and breastfeeding females. It is not known whether tecovirimat is present in breast milk [27]. If treatment is indicated in a pregnant or breastfeeding patient infected with the monkeypox virus, tecovirimat should be considered the first line of treatment for these patients. As mentioned before, information is limited on whether tecovirimat affects the fetus in the reproductive development; however, animal studies in the past showed no specific fetal effects even though the dose used in the animal study was 23 times higher than the dose used in humans [28,10]. CidofovirThis medication is effective against monkeypox in animal studies [27]. However, no significant clinical data exists on its efficacy toward monkeypox infection in humans. The mechanism of action of cidofovir includes converting cidofovir to its active metabolite called cidofovir diphosphonate. This cidofovir diphosphate then causes selective inhibition of viral DNA synthesis, suppressing virus replication. Cidofovir comes with a US boxed warning, including the possibility of severe nephrotoxicity. Severe acute renal failure resulting in dialysis can happen in as few as one to two doses of this medication. Renal functions must be monitored with each dose of cidofovir [29]. Patients who must be treated with this medication should also receive intravenous saline for rehydration and oral probenecid. Probenecid decreases the renal clearance of cidofovir by blocking the kidney's tubular secretions, reducing the incidence of nephrotoxicity [30].Other US boxed warnings: This medication can be carcinogenic and teratogenic based on animal studies. Also, patients are at risk of neutropenia with this medication; therefore, the patient's neutrophil count must be monitored when receiving this medication. There is a risk for metabolic acidosis along with hepatic impairment and pancreatitis. Cidofovir should be avoided in pregnant females as it can be teratogenic; however, if use is warranted, systemic therapy should be avoided during the first trimester if possible [31]. It is not known whether cidofovir can pass into the breastmilk or not at this time. However, breastfeeding is not recommended because of serious adverse reactions possible with this medication [29,31].Brincidofovir:This medication is similar to cidofovir but likely has fewer side effects. This medication is a lipid conjugate that is converted to cidofovir intracellularly, which is then further converted to cidofovir diphosphonate, an active metabolite of cidofovir. Cidofovir diphosphate causes selective viral DNA inhibition, suppressing the virus application. Significant side effects include hepatotoxicity. Upon initiating this medication, patients with hepatic impairment should closely monitor their liver functions. [32] If a patient develops hepatic impairment during the treatment, consider discontinuation if alanine transaminase (ALT) remains consistently high, >10 times the upper limit of normal [33,34]. Pregnant females should avoid taking this medication as in utero exposure to brincidofovir may harm the fetus. It is unknown if brincidofovir can transfer into breastmilk; therefore, breastfeeding is not recommended when the patient is on this medication [34].Trifluridine:This medication can be used to treat and prevent corneal and conjunctival involvement in patients with monkeypox lesions involving the eye. This medication comes in topical antibiotic drops or ointment, which can be applied every four hours for seven to 10 days [35,36]. No dosage adjustment is needed for patients with hepatic and kidney impairment. Trifluridine mechanism of action involves interference with replication of the virus by inhibiting thymidylate synthetase, reducing the viral load.PreventionFor prevention, a two-fold approach is needed. The first goal should be to promptly treat those infected and provide post-exposure management to minimize the onset of illness. The second goal will be at the public health and policy/ administrative level with increased funding and making diagnostic tests and vaccine availability a priority. Increased community awareness and wider surveillance of current cases and exposure is the first step toward preventing the spread [37,38]. There is a lack of evidence-based prevention methods, but we can utilize the knowledge learned from the COVID-19 pandemic [39]. From COVID-19, we learned that early diagnosis, quarantine for those with the infection, and open data sharing would be crucial for any community intervention to minimize the spread of any viral outbreaks [40]. Minimizing or avoiding stigmatization is needed to prevent discrimination and optimize disease response. Especially in the LGBTQ+ community and the public in general, aggressive educational campaigns regarding the transmission and spread will help minimize the stigma and, thereby, the hesitancy to seek help [41]. The stigmatization can also result in delays at the community, state, and even international levels, affecting political decision-making and resource allocation. In the past, Roess et al. noted educational activities to be effective in improving community-level knowledge and seeking professional advice [42]. Modifying the message delivery to match the current communication methods, including various forms of social media, should lead to similar results. The panic related to the current global health emergency, which is likely approaching the pandemic level, can be minimized with better education and unified messaging [39]. Key preventive measure is related to minimizing contact with the lesions, as close and prolonged contact appears to be the primary mode of transmission [11]. Social distancing from those with infection or post-exposure can also be considered useful, thereby minimizing possible respiratory transmission [12]. Avoiding sharing of beddings, towels, and clothes is needed [13].Pre-exposure prophylaxis vaccineThe Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) recommends pre-exposure prophylaxis by using the modified vaccinia Ankara (MVA) vaccine for individuals who are at high risk due to occupational exposure to orthopoxvirus infections [43], for example, clinical laboratory personnel or scientists who are performing diagnostic testing for orthopoxviruses and designated response team members who are at risk of occupational exposure as well [44]. Experts are even discussing the use of pre-exposure prophylaxis MVA vaccine for high-risk patients. These individuals may be able to get vaccines once we have enough supplies of the MVA vaccine [45].Post-exposure risk assessmentPeople should watch closely for symptoms for at least 21 days post-exposure with a monkeypox patient. If a person remains asymptomatic, they can resume their normal activities; however, if they start to experience symptoms, they should quarantine themselves and seek further medical attention from their primary care provider or the health department. There are three categories of risk of exposure [36].High-Risk ExposureCDC considers patients as high-risk exposure if they had: a) contact with infected patient's skin, mucous membranes, skin lesions, and/or body fluids, for example, sexual contact, contact with patient's saliva to the eye or oral cavity of an uninfected individual, contact with contaminated materials like clothes. b) Being within six feet of an infected patient undergoing procedures that increase the risk of creating aerosol from oral or skin lesions without wearing proper N95 and eye protection, for example, dental procedures, or shaking soiled infected clothes.Intermediate Risk ExposureA non-infected individual within six feet of an individual infected with monkeypox without wearing a mask for three hours or more is considered intermediate risk. Individuals should be wearing at least a surgical mask. An additional intermediate degree exposure is when a non-infected person using only gloves and not donning a gown comes in contact with an infected patient's bodily fluids, skin sores, or dirty clothing.Low-Risk ExposureCDC considers low risk when a non-infected individual comes in contact with an infected patient a) while taking all proper precautionary measures when entering a patient's room, b) without wearing eye protection regardless of the duration of exposure, and c) is within six feet for less than three hours, and not wearing a mask.CDC recommends that individuals exposed to the monkeypox virus refrain from donating organs, blood, or breastmilk for at least 21 days to ensure they do not develop symptoms [36].Post-exposure treatmentIndividuals exposed to the monkeypox virus should consult their public health authority, which will determine treatment plans depending on the exposure risk mentioned above. Individuals eligible for prophylactic vaccinations should be vaccinated within four days of exposure to achieve the maximum benefit. Even though the vaccine can be given for up to 14 days post-exposure, if given between four and 14 days post-exposure, it minimizes the symptoms and does not prevent infection [46].In individuals with high-risk exposure to monkeypox, per CDC guidelines, postexposure modified vaccinia Ankara (MVA) vaccination is required. Immunocompetent individuals may use the ACAM2000 vaccine as well. According to CDC guidelines [46], post-exposure prophylactic vaccination is determined case-by-case for individuals with intermediate risk exposure, including evaluation by likelihood of transmission. Post-exposure prophylactic vaccination is not indicated for individuals with a low risk of exposure.Vaccinia Immune GlobulinPatients who are immunocompromised and exposed to the monkeypox virus may require the use of vaccinia immune globulin. CDC must be contacted for this agent to be available for the patient if needed.Post-exposure vaccinationThere are two types of vaccination available that can reduce the risk of monkeypox infection.Modified Vaccinia Ankara (MVA) VaccineSold under the trade name Jynneos (also known as Imvamune or Imvanex) in the United States (US), it is a live, nonreplicating vaccine. This vaccination has an excellent safety profile and can even be used in immunocompromised patients and patients with skin disorders. This vaccine requires two doses subcutaneously, which are administered four weeks apart. This vaccination is made from the nonreplicating vaccinia virus. Common side effects of the MVA vaccine include headache, myalgia, pain at injection site, and lymphadenopathy that last only a few days post-vaccination [47].ACAM2000ACAM2000 is a replication-competent smallpox vaccine. This vaccination should be used only in healthy, immunocompetent, and nonpregnant patients with a high risk of exposure. This vaccination is associated with more side effects when compared to the MVA vaccine because ACAM2000 requires an infectious dose on a bifurcated sterile needle that is penetrated into the epidermis of the deltoid region of the arm about 15 times. This process is known as scarification. After two to five days of vaccination, a papule will form, becoming a vesicle after a few more days [48]. The vesicle reaches its maximum size in about one week to 10 days, and then a scab forms in two weeks, which then falls off. Patients vaccinated with ACAM2000 often complain of mild fever and lymphadenopathy for the first two weeks after vaccination.ConclusionsThe Orthopoxvirus, also known as monkeypox virus, was initially discovered in the 1950s. Previously, this virus was primarily confined to Central and West Africa. However, monkeypox virus infection has gradually expanded worldwide with the termination and eradication of the smallpox vaccine and virus. Therefore, on July 23, 2022, the WHO recently designated the monkeypox virus as a public health emergency of international concern (PHEIC). Attributed to the rise in cases, the CDC advises clinicians and other healthcare providers to remain vigilant and report to local health departments if they discover any patients infected with the monkeypox virus. These local health departments can then reach out to the CDC and formulate a strategy for individuals who had direct contact with these patients. Since this infection can spread via droplets or skin-to-skin contact, the healthcare professionals treating a patient suspected of monkeypox should use standard contact and droplet precautions. A crucial lesson is avoiding close contact with suspected patients to reduce transmission. Community education to maximize prevention efforts and destigmatizing to minimize barriers to seeking help are key to containment. 


Title: The recent re-emergence of human monkeypox: Would it become endemic beyond Africa?

IntroductionViral diseases continuously emerge and pose challenges to global health. Since the end of 2019, we have experienced a novel coronavirus, severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), which has caused a global pandemic to date. In the meantime, we also experience several viral outbreaks across the world, including influenza A viruses, Japanese encephalitis, Ebola virus, Yellow fever, and Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV) [1]. Another large, multicountry outbreak is currently reported in several European countries and the United States (US). The outbreak is due to the human monkeypox virus (hMPXV) that was previously only endemic in the western and central parts of Africa. Monkeypox is originally an ancient disease. Investigations of archived specimens of five species of African rope squirrel (Funisciurus sp.) collected across central Africa over the past 120 years demonstrated the earliest evidence of monkeypox infection in 1899 [2]. This finding suggests that the historical pox-like outbreaks were more likely due to monkeypox rather than variola (smallpox) viruses [2]. The emergence of outbreaks outside of Africa emphasizes the disease's global significance. In this review, we discuss briefly the monkeypox virus, its transmission, pathogenesis, and clinical manifestation, as well as its changing global epidemiology and possible driving factors of the current outbreak.A brief overview of the virology of the monkeypox virusMonkeypox virus belongs to the Orthopoxvirus genus within the Chordopoxvirinae subfamily of the Poxviridae family [3]. The Orthopoxvirus genus contains several viruses that pose a high risk to the human population, including variola virus (the cause of smallpox), vaccinia virus (the strains used for smallpox vaccination), camelpox, cowpox, and mousepox (ectromelia virus) [4]. The Orthopoxvirus infects a wide range of animals, from humans to domestic and wild animals [5]. New members of the Orthopoxvirus genus have been recently identified, such as the Alaskapox virus [6], Akhmeta virus [7], and Abatino virus [8].Monkeypox virus is a large, brick-shaped or ovoid, enveloped, double-stranded, linear DNA (dsDNA) virus of ∼190 kb with a diameter of approximately 200–250 nm (
Fig. 1). Monkeypox virus uniquely replicates within the cytoplasm of the infected cells rather than in the nucleus. This process is almost independent of the host cell’s cellular machinery [9]. The virus particle is extremely complex and contains more than 100 viral proteins. Of note, there are several enzymes found in the virus particle, largely involved in the genome replication [9]. During viral replication in the infected cells, two different forms of viral particles are produced, intracellular mature virus (IMV) and extracellular enveloped virus (EEV). IMV has only one inner membrane, while EEV has two membranes derived from the endoplasmic reticulum. Both forms are infectious, although they employ distinct mechanisms to infect susceptible cells [10].Fig. 1The structure of monkeypox virus.Fig. 1The viral genome contains more than 200 open reading frames (ORFs) [11]. Based on genomic sequencing analysis, there are two major clades of monkeypox virus, namely Congo Basin (Central African) and the West African clades [11], currently termed as monkeypox virus clade 1 and clade 2, respectively [12]. A new clade 3 contains monkeypox virus isolates that have been identified since 2017, and together with clade 2, they belong to the West African clade [12], [13]. Studies in cynomolgus monkeys revealed that the Congo Basin clade was more virulent than the West African clade [14]. Similarly, in infected patients, the Congo Basin clade had higher morbidity and mortality as well as viremia levels [11]. Molecular evolution analyses estimated that the monkeypox virus initiated its independent evolution around 3500 years ago, although the West African clade emerged more recently, about 600 years ago [15].The antigenic properties of Orthopoxvirus are capable of inducing both species-specific and cross-reacting antibodies. Smallpox vaccination with vaccinia virus confers an approximate 85% cross-protection immunity against monkeypox virus infection in humans [16]. However, following the eradication of smallpox in the 1980 s, widespread vaccination with live-attenuated vaccinia virus was discontinued. Consequently, most people under the age of 45 years may no longer be protected against Orthopoxvirus infections, including the monkeypox virus [17]
. After more than 40 years of smallpox eradication and declining immunity against smallpox, the monkeypox virus has become the most important Orthopoxvirus infection in humans [18], [19].Natural reservoirs and transmission of the monkeypox virusMonkeypox virus was first isolated in 1959 in cynomolgus monkeys maintained within an animal laboratory in Copenhagen, Denmark, following an outbreak of non-fatal pox-like diseases, hence its name [20]. The first diagnosis of human monkeypox case was reported in 1970 in Zaire (now in the Democratic Republic of Congo, DRC) during the final effort to eradicate smallpox. The patient was a male, 9-month old of age, and developed symptoms of smallpox-like disease [21]. Since then, the monkeypox has been endemic in the DRC as well as in the west and central African countries [22]. Beyond African countries, monkeypox cases were first recorded in a multistate outbreak in the US following the import of small exotic animal pets from Ghana in 2003 [23].Natural reservoirs for monkeypox virus transmission to humanMonkeypox is a zoonotic disease, i.e. primarily transmitted from animal to human, in contrast to variola virus, which is exclusively a human pathogen. Although first discovered in monkeys, the natural reservoir of the virus remains elusive [24]. Non-human primates serve as accidental hosts of the monkeypox virus [5]. In wild chimpanzees, distinct lineages of the monkeypox virus could concurrently circulate and might cause mild to severe respiratory syndrome with limited or absence of exanthema [25]. In a long-term observation of the chimpanzee population in Taï National Park, Ivory Coast, simultaneous outbreaks were observed in different forest areas, suggesting multiple sources of introduction from unknown reservoir hosts. Interestingly, an outbreak period in chimpanzees was preceded by years of the absence of the diseases, suggesting that certain ecological or environmental factors may cause a sudden surge of spillover events [25].Current data suggest that rodents are the primary reservoir of the virus [26]. Monkeypox virus is known to infect a wide range of rodents, including mice, rabbits, and hamsters [5]. During an outbreak investigation in the DRC, two of three rope squirrels (Funisciurus sp.) were positive for antibodies to Orthopoxviruses
[27]
. However, consumption or preparation of rope squirrels was not associated with an increased risk of contracting monkeypox infection [27]. Another study showed that pouched Gambian rats (Cricetomys gambianus) were susceptible to monkeypox virus infection and were capable of shedding viable virus particles, suggesting its role in maintaining the virus in the wildlife population [28]. Close or direct contact with the blood, body fluids, salivary/respiratory droplets, bites, or inoculation via mucocutaneous lesions and consumption of the animals (bushmeat) are the primary modes of zoonotic transmission events [3].Secondary human-to-human transmissionThe further spread of the monkeypox virus in the human population is because of subsequent human-to-human transmission event, which occurs via close contact with respiratory droplets, body fluids, skin lesion, or contaminated patient’s environment or items [3]. Thus, isolation of infected individuals is essential to reduce viral transmission [29]. The amount of viral DNA in the clinical samples (as determined by the PCR) was associated with infectivity. A Cq value of ≥ 35 was correlated with low or very low infectivity of the virus [30]. This report may support decision-making regarding the confirmed cases and their close contacts. Indirect transmission may occur since viable viruses have been successfully isolated from feces and flies associated with the infected chimpanzees [25]. In addition, orthopoxvirus virion is highly stable in the environment. Viable and infectious variola virus particles were successfully recovered from smallpox scabs after 13 years of storage at room temperature (15 °C-20 °C) [31].The primary zoonotic transmission event (close contact with wild and domestic animals) was followed by secondary human-to-human transmission, leading to outbreaks in the affected area [32]. There are three possible modes of human-to-human transmission of monkeypox: familial, healthcare-related (nosocomial), and transport-related [33]. However, monkeypox transmission is uncommon in healthcare settings. During the outbreak in 2003 in the US, the exposed healthcare workers did not develop signs and symptoms of monkeypox [34]. In the United Kingdom (UK), one case of nosocomial transmission became the first reported human-to-human transmission of monkeypox beyond African countries [35]. It was suggested that transmission was through contaminated bedding. Four of 134 contacts developed symptoms, and fortunately, all of them recovered [36].During the current outbreak, a possible reverse zoonotic transmission event (human-to-animal transmission) has been reported and may pose a serious challenge to stopping the transmission of the monkeypox virus. A monkeypox virus-infected dog was reported in France at 12 days after the symptom onset of the owner (a man, 44 years old) who had been tested positive for monkeypox virus. Sequencing analyses demonstrated that both viruses belonged to the hMPXV-1 clade 1, lineage B.1, with 100% homology of the 19.5 kbp sequenced [37]. Thus, there is a high possibility that the infection was acquired through human transmission via close contact with his dog [37].The pathogenesis of the monkeypox virus infectionThe clinical features of monkeypox infection in humans are highly associated with the acquisition route, with the respiratory tract and the oral cavity as the common entry route. In an experimental model of monkeypox virus infection in cynomolgus monkeys (Macaca fascicularis), epithelial cells in the lower respiratory tract were the primary target of infection following aerosol exposure [38]. Tonsil, mediastinal, and mandibular lymph nodes may also serve as additional sites of primary infections, from which the virus can disseminate through lymphatogenous spread. Systemic dissemination via blood (haematogenous route) was acquired through monocytic cells-associated viremia and led to the development of characteristic lesions in the skin, oral mucosa, gastrointestinal, and reproductive tracts [38]. In the blood, monkeypox virus induced massive expansion of natural killer (NK) cells but suppressed their cytotoxic and cytokine production capacity [39]. In mousepox infection models, secondary viremia may occur following primary dissemination of the virus in the spleen and liver [40].Monkeypox virus could also be transmitted via sexual contact [41]. Monkeypox virus DNA has been detected in rectal swabs, semen, and feces, with the median time of persistence of 8.3, 11.4, and 9.4, respectively; thus, increasing the likelihood of acquisition through sexual contacts [42], [43]. In a case report, it was reported that genital rash occurred at 5 days after sexual contact, followed by fever and lymphadenopathy at 3 days after rash onset [44]. Accordingly, the presence of genital and perianal lesions was related to the role in sexual intercourse [45]. In a prospective cross-sectional study in Spain, all patients had systemic symptoms after the primary acquisition of contact during sexual activities [46]. Further studies are urgently required to identify the reservoirs of the virus in the reproductive tissue and the mechanisms of its systemic dissemination.The clinical presentation of the monkeypox virus infectionThe incubation period of monkeypox virus infection is about 7–17 days and can be longer until 21 days. The classical clinical presentation of monkeypox virus infection is similar to smallpox and varicella. Thus, clinical diagnosis may be difficult, particularly in resource-limited settings of supporting diagnostic tools [47]. Vesiculopustular rash distributed in the face, legs, trunk, arms, palms, and genitalia is the most prominent symptom. In many cases, the rash starts from the face and could spread to other parts of the body, for instance, genital areas [48]. The rash develops in various stages and has similarities with syphilis, chancroid, herpes simplex virus infection, and chickenpox. Afterwards, the lesion forms a scab, and the scab then falls off [47].Other accompanying symptoms include fever, headache, pruritus, myalgia, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, and conjunctivitis. Fever may precede the development of rash in a sub-group of patients and vice versa [32], [49]. The interval between rash and fever is about two days [50]. Smallpox was not associated with lymphadenopathy [47]. Viral DNA could be detected in the blood (viremia), urine, and upper respiratory swabs [51]. Of note, prolonged PCR positivity in the blood and upper respiratory tract samples has been observed in monkeypox patients, and consequently, challenges the infection control measures to prevent viral spread [51].The illness is mostly mild and could recover within three weeks from the onset period. The treatment is mainly supportive. Two available oral antiviral drugs approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for smallpox, brincidofovir and tecovirimat, have been used as off-label drugs for monkeypox treatment [51]. Unfortunately, secondary bacterial infections of the skin lesion, followed by sepsis, may occur. Other complications include gastroenteritis, bronchopneumoniae, encephalitis, and fetal death [49]. In endemic countries, coinfections with varicella-zoster virus (VZV) are quite common and may influence the clinical severity [52]. During the outbreak of monkeypox in Nigeria in 2017–2018, the case fatality rate (CFR) was approximately 6% [32]. In the UK cases between 2018 and 2021, no deaths were reported [51]. A recent meta-analysis estimated that about 35% of monkeypox cases were hospitalized, with approximately 4% fatalities among the hospitalized cases [53].Pre-outbreak situations of monkeypox virus infections in humans (1970–2021)A recent systematic review of peer-reviewed and grey literature (until 7 September 2020) showed that the reported human monkeypox cases had increased significantly since the 1970 s. Between 1970 and 1979, confirmed and probable human monkeypox cases were reported from Sierra Leone (n = 1), Liberia (n = 4), Côte d′Ivoire (n = 1), Nigeria (n = 3), Cameroon (n = 1), and the DRC (n = 38). Between 2010 and 2019, the total number of confirmed, probable, and/or possible human monkeypox cases remarkably increased. During this period, the DRC reported more than 18,000 cases. The human monkeypox was reported in 10 African countries (Sierra Leone, Liberia, Cote d′Ivoire, Nigeria, Cameroon, the DRC, Central African Republic [CAR], Gabon, South Sudan, and Congo) and four countries beyond Africa [the US (n = 47 in 2003 across six states), the UK (n = 4 in 2018 and 2019), Israel (n = 1 in 2018), and Singapore (n = 1 in 2019)] [22].Most cases in endemic countries were due to infections of the Central African clade. However, beyond Africa, the cases were due to the West African clade, and they were import- and travel-related cases leading to sporadic outbreaks [22], [35]. Across all countries, the estimated CFR was 8.7% (95% CI: 7.0%−10.8%). The CFR for the Central African clade was significantly higher than the West African clade (10.6% vs. 3.6%). Of note, the median age at presentation has increased from 4 years in the 1970 s to 21 years in the 2010–2019 period [22].Currently, Nigeria is experiencing an ongoing monkeypox outbreak. In 2021, the total number of confirmed cases was 34, while up to April 2022, 15 confirmed cases have been recorded [54]. This led to several imported cases of monkeypox to the UK and the US during the upsurge of Delta variant of SARS-CoV-2 [55]. In May 2021, an imported case of the West African clade was reported from the UK. The index case had a travel history from Delta State, Nigeria. Secondary transmission occurred within two family members [56]. Another imported case of the West African clade was reported from Dallas, Texas, the US in July 2021. The index case was an early middle-aged man with less than one week of travel history to Nigeria. Fortunately, no secondary transmission occurred [57]. In the US, an imported case was also reported from Maryland in a 28-year-old man travelling from Lagos, Nigeria [58].Current outbreak situations (May, 2022 to January 5, 2023)On May 7, 2022, the United Kingdom Health Security Agency (UKHSA) reported the first confirmed monkeypox case in 2022 in Britain, a non-endemic country of monkeypox. The case had a travel history to Nigeria as the endemic country on May 3, 2022 and previously experienced a rash on April 29, 2022. A confirmed case is a suspected or probable case and is proved with monkeypox virus detection by real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and/or sequencing [59]. The monkeypox virus PCR was performed toward this case by UKHSA Rare and Imported Pathogen Laboratory on May 6, 2022 from a vesicle swab specimen. Then, on May 13, 2022, two other confirmed cases in the same household were reported. However, this family cluster case had no association with the first case recorded on May 7, 2022. On May 15, 2022, four other confirmed cases were reported in the UK, and these cases also have no links to the first case (reported on May 7, 2022) and the family cluster case (reported on May 13, 2022). These four cases were men who have sex with men (MSM) and were detected when they were examined in genitourinary medicine clinics [60].From May 7 to May 25, 2022, there were 90 confirmed cases in the UK [61]. On May 18, 2022, Portugal also reported 14 confirmed cases of men. On May 19, 2022, seven confirmed cases were reported in Spain [60]. In addition, on May 18, 2022, a confirmed case of monkeypox was also detected in the US resident who travelled from Canada to the US [62]. In Australia, the first monkeypox case was reported in a male, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-positive individual with travel history to Europe. He developed a genital rash five days after unprotected anal intercourse with four males during his visit in Europe [44]
. Between May 17 and May 22, 2022, Italy also reported four monkeypox cases, all of them were young adult MSM males, two of them were HIV positive [63]
.
The number of cases from the period of May 7, 2022 to January 5, 2023 is described in
Fig. 2. Sequence analysis showed that the West African clade is responsible for the current outbreak [44], [63], [64]
. Until January 5, 2023, there were 84,318 confirmed cases reported worldwide. From those cases, 83,127 cases were found in regions which have not previously reported monkeypox (103 countries), and 1191 cases were detected in regions which have historically reported monkeypox cases (7 countries). Furthermore, the number of death was 74 cases in 17 countries, such as Argentina (1), Belgium (1), Brazil (14), Cameroon (3), Chile (2), Cuba (1), Czechia (1), Ecuador (2), Ghana (4), India (1), Mexico (4) Mozambique (1), Nigeria (7), Peru (8), Spain (3), Sudan (1), and United States of America (20) [65].Fig. 2Geographical distribution of confirmed cases of human monkeypox virus infection (up to January 5, 2023).Fig. 2What are the underlying factors associated with the current outbreaks?Silent, undetected chain of transmission events preceding the outbreaksMonkeypox virus infection in humans is endemic only in the west and central Africa. Previous cases of monkeypox virus outside of African countries were always associated with travel to these endemic areas. Those imported cases were due to the West African clade, which was known to have lower fatality and less human-to-human transmission rates. In the current multi-country outbreak, West African clades were also identified among confirmed cases. A previous systematic review also showed no emergence of new strains of the monkeypox virus [24]. In addition, the current outbreak appears to be spreading in different ways than previous outbreaks outside of Africa.Sequence analysis of the virus available at this moment indicated that the current outbreak originates from a single origin and is closely associated with the exported virus from Nigeria to the UK, Singapore, and Israel in 2018 and 2019 [59], [66]. This circumstance reminds us with a human case in Cameroon in 2018 after no reported monkeypox cases since 1989. Sequence analysis showed that the virus was the West African clade and was closely related to the monkeypox virus isolated from an outbreak in Nigeria from 2017 to 2018. While in 1989 cases, it was due to the Congo Basin clade. Interestingly, there was no travel history to Nigeria nor interaction with travellers from Nigeria of the infected case. This finding may suggest a “cryptic” transmission event of the monkeypox virus in Cameroon before the reported human case, although an importation from Nigeria could not be completely ruled out [67]. Noteworthy, another serological study in Cameroon demonstrated that silent, undetected transmissions of asymptomatic animals and humans may occur until certain levels that could be recognized by a surveillance system [68]. In line, it was shown that the monkeypox virus maintained its circulation in animal hosts in Ghana, but no apparent human cases were identified [69], until it was exported to the US and precipitated the outbreak [22]. The fact that monkeypox cases were found in patients who had no obvious association each other shows that the virus might have silently circulated for a given period of time preceding the outbreaks [70].Are there any genetic determinants of the current outbreak?Recent studies reported comprehensive analyses of the human monkeypox virus sequences obtained from the past to the current outbreaks. A maximum-likelihood tree demonstrated clustering of the sequences into three major clusters: (1) MPXV clade 1 contained sequences derived from 1970 to 2017 outbreaks in Central Africa; (2) MPXV clade 2 contained sequences derived from 1970 to 2017 outbreaks in different countries; and (3) MPXV clade 3 contained sequences derived from the last two outbreaks (2017–2022). Several sub-lineages have been identified in clade 3, including A.1, A.1.1., A.2 and B.1 [12]. Interestingly, all genomes obtained from the current 2022 outbreaks were clustered in B.1. lineage of clade 3 and emerged in Europe as early as March 2022 [12], [13]. These studies indicated that the current outbreak had a single origin and clearly showed diversification of monkeypox virus following sustained transmission in non-endemic regions.Monkeypox virus is a DNA virus which commonly has a slower mutation rate compared to an RNA virus, thus the genome is relatively stable [71]. It was estimated that the mutation rate of Orthopoxvirus was± (4−6) x 10−6 substitutions/site/year [72]. However, it has been shown that poxviruses can quickly adapt to changing environments in the infected host (human) cells despite their low mutation rate [73]. Interestingly, seven single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and one deletion were observed among sequenced viruses from the UK, US, and Portugal, indicating ongoing microevolution of the circulating viruses responsible for the current outbreaks [66]. However, it is hard to believe that these genetic changes are associated with selective advantage by increasing the transmission capability of the virus. Three non-synonymous substitutions in the surface glycoprotein B21R (D209N, P722S, and M1741I) could provide selective advantage for the monkeypox virus by enhancing its transmission capacity [12]. Amino acid variabilities in H3L, another viral envelope protein, between variola and monkeypox viruses may also associate with virus adaptation to humans [74].It is important to note that sustained human-to-human transmission during the current outbreak may provide sufficient time and opportunities for the monkeypox virus to improve and fine-tune its adaptation and specificity in the human host, as we have seen in SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern (VOC). Further comprehensive studies are required to investigate any genetic changes that may alter the behavior of the virus.Treatment and preventive strategiesTreatment strategiesPain management and supportive treatment could be a strategy for treating monkeypox. Topical and systemic medications, including non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), acetaminophen, or lidocaine, can be used to relieve pain in monkeypox cases. For severe pain, gabapentin or opioids can be prescribed with caution of the side effects [75]. Furthermore, supportive treatments should be given to monkeypox patients. Mucous membrane and compromised skin should be cleaned with antiseptic, protected with light dressing, and treated with mupironic acid. In addition, systemic antibiotics in secondary infection cases could be needed. Monkeypox patients can suffer from dehydration due to nausea, vomiting, or poor appetite. Thus, they should obtain nutritional care and rehydration therapy, for instance, oral fluids, intravenous fluids, and healthy diet. Symptom-relieving medications also should be prescribed for fever, itching, vomiting, malaise, or symptoms regarding the patient’s condition [76].To date, specific antiviral treatment for monkeypox approved by the US FDA is not available. However, antiviral drugs for smallpox might be beneficial for treating monkeypox, e.g., tecovirimat, brincidofovir, Vaccinia Immune Globulin Intravenous (VIGIV), and cidofovir [77]. A phase 3 clinical trial is currently being conducted to evaluate the efficacy of tecovirimat for monkeypox treatment (NCT05534984). A retrospective observational study in the UK revealed that one monkeypox patient treated with tecovirimat (600 mg per oral, twice daily for two weeks) experienced no adverse effects. The patient also had a shorter duration of illness and viral shedding than the other patients, with ten days of hospitalization [51]. According to the FDA’s review, brincidofovir is considered for monkeypox patients with severe disease or contraindications for tecovirimat. VIGIV can be considered for severe cases of monkeypox, and clinicians should request the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Cidofovir is effective against Orthopoxvirus based on in vitro as well as animal studies. Yet, it cannot be used with brincidofovir [77]. Large clinical trials to assess the efficacy of antiviral therapy against monkeypox in humans are still needed.Prevention and vaccination strategiesThe preventive measures for monkeypox could be enhanced by raising awareness about its associated risk factors. Human-to-human transmission could be reduced by active surveillance and contact tracing. Health providers with close contact with patients and laboratory staff handling specimens should follow infection control precautions appropriately. In addition, risks of zoonotic transmission should be reduced by using protective equipment during contact with wild animals and consuming cooked meat. Furthermore, isolating infected animals and restricting animal trade, such as rodents and non-human primates, could prevent monkeypox transmission [41].The smallpox vaccination is also effective in preventing monkeypox, with 85% of efficacy [16]. Currently, there are three smallpox vaccines. However, there are only two vaccines that are licensed by the US FDA, i.e. ACAM2000 and JYNNEOS. ACAM2000 contains replication-competent vaccinia virus and is indicated for active immunization against smallpox disease in people with high risks of smallpox infection. ACAM2000 is a single-dose vaccine that is administered percutaneously. Meanwhile, JYNNEOS is a live-attenuated vaccine and can be used for populations 18 years old and above with immunodeficiencies, such as HIV patients. JYNNEOS is administered subcutaneously with two doses, 4 weeks apart. ACAM2000 has more side effects than JYNNEOS and it is not recommended for immunocompromised people [78]. The other smallpox vaccine is an investigational vaccine, Aventis Pasteur Smallpox Vaccine (APSV), which might be used under Emergency Use Authorization (EUA). People at risk are recommended for smallpox vaccination, for instance, research laboratory staff, clinical laboratory staff handling tests for Orthopoxviruses, and healthcare personnel who treat patients with vaccinia virus infection [79].According to the interim guidance by WHO on November 16, 2022, mass vaccination is not required and not recommended at the moment. Public health measures could curb monkeypox cases, for instance, surveillance, contact tracing, early diagnosis, and isolation. Vaccination should be considered as an additional measure. WHO also recommends that member states share vaccine doses with countries with limited vaccine supply [80].Vaccination challengesInequity is one of the challenges in vaccination for monkeypox. The hindrances of vaccination include geographic location and transportation, education, racism, language, vaccine hesitancy, and lack of trust from government [81]. Since September 15, 2022, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has developed “The Monkeypox Vaccine Equity Pilot Program” to increase vaccine access in most impacted communities with monkeypox virus, for instance Black/African American and Hispanic/Latino gay, bisexual, and MSM. The examples of the pilot projects are ‘Vaccine clinics’ at pharmacies in rural areas, events in LGBTQ+ concerts, and clinics for MSM who are not reached by vaccine administration channels [82]. Post-exposure vaccination of high-risk contacts of monkeypox has a challenge in contact tracing because of unwillingness to disclose the sexual partners due to stigma [83].Would the monkeypox virus become endemic beyond Africa?The monkeypox virus might occupy the ecological, epidemiological, or immunological niche left by smallpox following its eradication [17]. A recent systematic review found that the median age of patients has changed from 4 years in the 1970 s to 21 years in the 2010–2019 period. From the 1970 s to the 1990 s, all fatal cases were among children< 10 years. However, there were 37.5% (6/16) of deaths found among children< 10 years of age in the last two decades (2000–2019) [22]. Those who were considered to have received smallpox vaccination had a lower incidence of monkeypox than those who were presumed unvaccinated [50], [84]. Thus, the current outbreaks may represent a real effect of diminished immunity against monkeypox at the population levels as the unvaccinated individuals become older. The currently available live-attenuated vaccines could be considered as pre- or post-exposure prophylaxis for contacts and health workers [62]. People with high-risk contacts with confirmed cases are suggested for self-isolation at home until 21 days [61], [85].The available data highly suggests that human-to-human transmission is currently happening and the existence of unconnected clusters [64]. It raises questions about whether monkeypox would replace smallpox and become a significant human pathogen globally. Another distinguishing feature is that a considerable number of cases have been identified in MSM, though not all, and many of these cases are being detected in sexually transmitted infection (STI) clinics [63], [64], [86]. Although monkeypox has never been recognized as a sexually transmitted infection, it could be transmitted by direct contact during sexual activities via genital or perianal lesions. Accordingly, seminal fluid of the infected patients in Italy was positive for the viral DNA [63]. Since the virus is apparently less transmissible than SARS-CoV-2, it should be easier to contain. However, a major factor of endemicity is that monkeypox virus could spill back to an unidentified animal reservoir widely distributed outside Africa and then establish new reservoirs in these areas. Indeed, experimental infections of ground squirrels (Spermophilus tridecemlineatus) obtained from the North America showed that this species was susceptible to monkeypox virus infection [87].In addition, the possibility of spillback events is supported by the fact that monkeypox can infect a wide range of animals. This kind of spillback event has been identified in SARS-CoV-2 [88], [89] and influenza A virus [90]. If this truly happens in the monkeypox virus as reported in a current study [37], the virus could maintain its continuous circulation in animals during the endemic or inter-epidemic period. The likelihood of human infection will then depend on cross-protective immunity derived from (smallpox) vaccination or from natural infection to variola or other Orthopoxviruses. If the monkeypox case becomes endemic, one of the main challenges in preventing the case is the low level of understanding about monkeypox amongst health care workers [91].ConclusionThe current monkeypox outbreak is an alarming situation for global health since this is the first large, multicountry outbreak outside Africa with no travel-association to endemic countries or importations of infected animals. The number of suspected and confirmed monkeypox cases keeps increasing. Another distinguishing characteristic is that a significant number of cases were found among MSM, raising awareness of whether the virus has established continuous circulation in a specific population. Efforts are ongoing to unravel the social and epidemiological links between cases and more importantly, the origin and driving factors of the current, mysterious outbreak, including viral and host genetic determinants, human behavior, animal reservoirs, as well as environmental and ecologic changes. In line, increased active case detection, immediate isolation, contact tracing, and postexposure vaccination should be performed to promptly contain the outbreak. Last but not least, enhancing our global preparedness is crucial to build disease surveillance and response capacities to monkeypox.Declaration of Competing InterestThe authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
